title: Step_filter_missing enhancements
description:
Regarding `step_filter_missing()`: This is a great addition but the name implies it is removing rows rather than columns. Compare with `step_filter()`. Perhaps a different name? `step_excess_missing()`?

**Can I suggest a related feature enhancement?** If the function has both a variable missingness threshold AND an observation missingness threshold then both rows and columns can be removed. Since the order of doing these should always be 
1. variables first, 
2. observations second, 
to ensure the maximum number of observations are always retained. Having these two operations in a single recipe step ensures the order is optimal. 

I find that, depending on the quality of imputation, varying the value for the observation missingness threshold allows the model's performance metric to be optimised. I hope you are following my thinking. 

Keep up the good work. I am a fan of **recipes**.

title: Error: The following cols are missing from `new_data` after #865
description:
## The problem

When creating a recipe from the data (not formula; using `update_role()`) and adding it to a workflow with a model overriding the formula (using `workflows::add_model(spec, formula = <formula>)`), `recipes` complains about missing cols in the `new_data` that are actually not missing and not used in the `<formula>`. The example bellow works fine before #865.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(reprex)
library(parsnip)
library(recipes)
library(workflows)

data(ad_data, package = "modeldata")

ad_rec <-
  ad_data %>%
  recipe() %>%
  update_role(Class, new_role = "outcome") %>%
  update_role(tau, VEGF, new_role = "predictor") %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

ad_spec <-
  logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm")

ad_wf <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(ad_rec) %>%
  add_model(ad_spec, formula = Class ~ tau + VEGF) %>%
  fit(data = ad_data)

predict(ad_wf, ad_data[1:4,])
#> Error:
```

title: Add step id to term_info
description:
## Feature - add the unique step id or number to `term_info`

`term_info` contains useful information about the source (generic), type, role and name of the model terms.  One piece of information that could be added that I would find useful is the step id, number, or some identifier that relates the variable name to the step that generated/modified/removed it. `term_info` currently does not include it.  Happy to do a pull request if desired to update `term_info` .

``` r
suppressMessages(library(recipes))

n <- 10
start <- as.Date('1999/01/01')
end <- as.Date('1999/01/10')

df <- data.frame(x = runif(n),
                 index = 1:n,
                 day = seq(start, end, by = "day"))

rec <- recipe(~ ., data = df) |>
  step_lag(index, day, lag = 0:1) |>
  step_center(index) |>
  step_mutate(index_2 = index * 2) |>
  prep(df)

rec$term_info
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>   variable    type    role      source  
#>   <chr>       <chr>   <chr>     <chr>   
#> 1 x           numeric predictor original
#> 2 index       numeric predictor original
#> 3 day         date    predictor original
#> 4 lag_0_index numeric predictor derived 
#> 5 lag_0_day   date    predictor derived 
#> 6 lag_1_index numeric predictor derived 
#> 7 lag_1_day   date    predictor derived 
#> 8 index_2     numeric predictor derived
```

title: `step_convolve` feature
description:
## Feature

This feature request is inspired by the `dlnm` package.  I propose a `step_convolve` which convolves a feature column(s) with a list of kernel(s).  My primary application uses large matrices where the speed of the convolution method is important to consider (FFT based when possible (no `NA` and a regular series)).  A small example application is shown below where a smoothly varying input kernel is recovered using a reduced number of regressors. 
``` r
library(splines)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(broom)

set.seed(123)

# kernel
n_data   <- 200
kern_len <- 15
kern     <- 0.8^(0:kern_len) * 0.5
plot(kern, type = 'o', pch = 20, col = '#b47846', lwd = 2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/S0aFbzn.png)

``` r

# data - two series: one is a lagged version of the other with scaling
input  <- rnorm(n_data)
output <- convolve(input, c(rep(0, n_data - length(kern)), rev(kern)))[-1]
input  <- input[-length(input)]
plot(input, type = 'l', col = '#b47846', lwd = 2, ylab = 'values',
     main = 'orange is input, blue is output')
points(output, type = 'l', col = 'steelblue', lwd = 2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/pUEYcSY.png)

``` r

# natural spline basis with 4 terms
sp <- ns(0:kern_len, knots = c(1, 6), intercept = TRUE)


# regression matrix (This would be the focus of the step)
#   a list of kernels and a feature are provided to the step
#   special care to make sure it is performant
m <- do.call(cbind, lapply(0:kern_len, function(k) dplyr::lag(x = input, n = k)))
m <- m %*% sp


# regression deconvolution
fit <- lm(output~m-1)
plot(fit$residuals, type = 'l', col = '#b47846')
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/gwyIfea.png)

``` r
glance(fit)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 12
#>   r.squared adj.r.squared   sigma statistic p.value    df logLik    AIC    BIC
#>       <dbl>         <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1      1.00          1.00 0.00248  3810175.       0     4   845. -1680. -1664.
#> # … with 3 more variables: deviance <dbl>, df.residual <int>, nobs <int>
tidy(fit)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   term  estimate std.error statistic   p.value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 m1       0.232  0.000207     1120.   0      
#> 2 m2      -0.167  0.000203     -824. Inf.e-324
#> 3 m3       0.594  0.000210     2835.   0      
#> 4 m4      -0.325  0.000182    -1789.   0

# kernels (the two kernels are basically indistinguishable)
co <- coefficients(fit)
plot(kern, type = 'o', pch = 20, col = '#b47846', lwd = 2,
     main = 'Orange is the input kernel, blue is deconvolved result')
points(sp %*% co, type = 'o', pch = 20, col = 'steelblue',  lwd = 2)
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/GWhVTms.png)

title: Add warning if step_normalize introduces NaN's in column
description:
## Background
For columns with zero variance, `step_normalize()` replaces the whole column with `NaN`'s. I had a very hard time debugging this when trying to feed the data to a model and got an `Error: Missing data in columns:`.

## Reproducible example
``` R
x1 <- sample(c(NaN,5,10),300,replace=TRUE)
x2 <- sample(1,300,replace=TRUE)
x3 <- sample(c(0,1),300,replace=TRUE)
df1 <- data.frame(x1,x2,x3)

dfsplits <- initial_split(df1, strata = x3)
df_train <- training(dfsplits)
df_test  <- testing(dfsplits)

df_recipe <-
  recipe(x1 ~ ., data = df_train) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

df_recipe %>%
  prep(df_train) %>%
  bake(df_test)

# A tibble: 76 x 3
      x2     x3    x1
   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
 1   NaN  0.946     5
 2   NaN -1.05    NaN
 3   NaN  0.946     5
 4   NaN -1.05      5
 5   NaN -1.05     10
 6   NaN  0.946    10
 7   NaN  0.946    10
 8   NaN  0.946    10
 9   NaN  0.946   NaN
10   NaN -1.05     10
# ... with 66 more rows
```

``` R
df_model <- rand_forest(mtry=50,trees=150) %>%
            set_engine('ranger',importance='impurity') %>%
            set_mode('regression')

df_workflow <- 
  workflow() %>% 
  add_model(df_model) %>% 
  add_recipe(df_recipe)

df_workflow %>% 
  fit(data = df_train)
# Error: Missing data in columns: x2.
```
I now know that this can be mitigated for this particular case with `step_zv()` to remove the zero-variance column, but it would be great if there had been any indication that `step_normalize()` introduced the `NaN` values.

title: step_filter() with / without roles
description:
`step_filter()` leads to error in train
> Error in { : task 1 failed - "replacement has 3107 rows, data has 1606"

**Example 1: With formula**
```r
data(okc)
rec_okc <- recipe(Class ~ ., okc) %>%
    step_filter(location == "san francisco")
prepped <- prep(rec_okc, training = okc) %>% juice
sum(prepped$location == "san francisco")
sum(prepped$location != "san francisco")
fit_okc <- train(rec_okc %>% step_rm(location), 
                 data = okc, 
                 method = "glm",
                 family = "binomial",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 1))
```

**Example 2: No formula**

```r
data(okc)
okc$height[c(1, 34234,22322,2,22)] <- NA
rec_okc <- recipe(okc) %>%
    step_factor2string(all_nominal()) %>%
    step_filter(location == "san francisco") %>%
    update_role(diet, height, new_role = "predictor") %>%
    update_role(Class, new_role = "outcome") %>%
    step_medianimpute(height) %>%
    step_mutate(diet = fct_explicit_na(diet, "missing")) %>%
    step_string2factor(has_role("predictor"), -has_type("date"), -has_type("numeric")) %>%
    step_dummy(has_role("predictor"), -has_type("date"), -has_type("numeric"))

prep(rec_okc,  okc, retain= TRUE) %>% juice
fit_okc <- train(rec_okc %>% step_rm(-all_predictors(), -all_outcomes()), 
                 data = okc, 
                 method = "glm",
                 family = "binomial",
                 trControl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", repeats = 1))
```

Was also surprised that you cannot use other variables in recipe, once outcome and predictor roles defined in initial formula:, i.e. following also gives error

```r
data(okc)
rec_okc <- recipe(Class ~ diet, okc) %>%
    step_filter(location == "san francisco")
prepped <- prep(rec_okc, training = okc) %>% juice
```

> Error in location == "san francisco" :

title: Inverse transformations
description:
In the **scikit-learn** world, preprocessors such as [StandardScaler](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html) or [LabelEncoder](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder.html#sklearn.preprocessing.LabelEncoder) have _inverse_transform_ method, which transforms the data back to the original representation.  It can be useful e.g. while working on classifcation task or regression with scaled target variable. For the latter one, scikit-learn has even a dedicated [TransformedTargetRegressor](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.compose.TransformedTargetRegressor.html#sklearn.compose.TransformedTargetRegressor) class which facilitates building pipelines composed of regressor and two-way target/output transformation.

My proposal is to introduce an additional verb to easily handle such cases, say _invert_. It could work as shown below:

```r
library(recipes, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
#> Warning: package 'recipes' was built under R version 4.0.5
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> Warning: replacing previous import 'vctrs::data_frame' by 'tibble::data_frame'
#> when loading 'dplyr'
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

iris_df <- as.data.frame(iris)

iris_recipe <- 
  recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris_df) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_dummy(Species, one_hot = TRUE) %>% 
  prep()

(iris_df_transformed <-
  iris_recipe %>% 
  bake(new_data = iris_df))
#> # A tibble: 150 x 7
#>    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species_setosa
#>           <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>          <dbl>
#>  1       -0.898      1.02          -1.34       -1.31              1
#>  2       -1.14      -0.132         -1.34       -1.31              1
#>  3       -1.38       0.327         -1.39       -1.31              1
#>  4       -1.50       0.0979        -1.28       -1.31              1
#>  5       -1.02       1.25          -1.34       -1.31              1
#>  6       -0.535      1.93          -1.17       -1.05              1
#>  7       -1.50       0.786         -1.34       -1.18              1
#>  8       -1.02       0.786         -1.28       -1.31              1
#>  9       -1.74      -0.361         -1.34       -1.31              1
#> 10       -1.14       0.0979        -1.28       -1.44              1
#> # ... with 140 more rows, and 2 more variables: Species_versicolor <dbl>,
#> #   Species_virginica <dbl>

invert <- function(x, ...){
  UseMethod("invert")
}


invert.step <- function(x, data, ...) {
  rlang::abort(
    paste0(
      "No `invert` method for a step with classes: ",
      paste0(class(x), collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}


invert.step_normalize <- function(x, data, ...){

  mapping <- Map(as.character, rlang::exprs(...))

  if (length(mapping) == 0) {
    .cols  <- names(x$means)
    mapping <- .cols
    names(mapping) <- .cols
  }
  
  # Column name
  cn <- function (x) mapping[[x]]

  data <- 
    data %>% 
    mutate(across(
      all_of(names(mapping)), 
      ~ .x  * x$sds[[cn(cur_column())]] + x$means[[cn(cur_column())]]
    ))
  
  data
}


invert(iris_recipe$steps[[1]], data = iris_df_transformed)
```

title: discretize( ..., keep_na = T) does not work when there's NA (related to issue #127)
description:
## The problem
I had trouble running `recipes::step_discretize` to predictors with `NA` values. This problem is related to issue #127.

## Reproducible example
Using the example in `?recipes::discretize`:

```
library(modeldata)

discretize(biomass$carbon, cuts = 2, infs = FALSE, keep_na = T, na.rm = T)
```

title: step_holiday fails with NA values
description:
## The problem

The `step_holiday` function seems to return errors during baking/juicing in the presence of NA values. For example

## Reproducible example
```
library(recipes)

dd <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(c("2021-12-04", "2021-12-25", NA, "2021-12-27"))
)

recipe(~date, data=dd) %>% 
  step_holiday(date) %>% 
  prep() %>% 
  juice()

# Error in if (rng.nch[1] != rng.nch[2]) stop("'charvec' has non-NA entries of different number of characters") : 
#   missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```
Tested with `recipes_0.1.16`

## Possible solution

The problem seems to be with the `is_holiday` function. It's passing a unique vector of years to the `timeDate::holiday()` function but that vector can include NA values which end up throwing the error the `timeDate::holiday()` code. It would be better to omit NA years (possibly checking to make sure there is at least one NA-year). It probably also makes sense to propagate the NA values in the returned indicator columns. One possible solution is 

```
is_holiday <- function(hol, dt) {
  # ~~ add na.omit() here to drop NA values ~~
  hdate <- holiday(year = unique(year(na.omit(dt))), Holiday = hol)
  hdate <- as.Date(hdate)
  out <- rep(0, length(dt))
  out[dt %in% hdate] <- 1
  # ~~ carry forward missing values ~~
  out[is.na(dt)] <- NA
  out
}
```
This updated version of the function would return
```
# A tibble: 4 x 4
  date       date_LaborDay date_NewYearsDay date_ChristmasDay
  <date>             <dbl>            <dbl>             <dbl>
1 2021-12-04             0                0                 0
2 2021-12-25             0                0                 1
3 NA                    NA               NA                NA
4 2021-12-27             0                0                 0
```
If that seems like a reasonable solution, I could prepare a pull request.

title: check distribution shift continuous variables
description:
A learned effect can be invalid when the distribution of the feature as a whole shifts. For instance if we regress the square feet of a house to its price, we would systematically overestimate house size when house prices rise.

How should we check for distribution shifts? Simple implementation might be allow a location measure like mean or median to shift only with a certain proportion of the total range. Or allow it to shift by a factor of the standard deviation. Alternatively, look at distributions as a whole, for instance with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

title: check distribution shift categorical variables
description:
Same rationale as #112, but for categoricals. 

Also here, make up our minds over how to implement. Chi-squared test might be an option.

title: `fresh = TRUE` doesn't reset term_info
description:
Extracted from https://github.com/tidymodels/workflows/issues/69

With `fresh = TRUE`, the recipe isn't correctly reset before the steps are processed.

```r
library(recipes)
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(212)

circle_example2 <- themis::circle_example %>%
  mutate(category = rep(c("A", "B"), length.out = n())) %>%
  as_tibble()

head(circle_example2)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 4
#>       x     y class  category
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <fct>  <chr>   
#> 1  2.59 10.6  Rest   A       
#> 2  9.71  6.83 Circle B       
#> 3  9.53 11.6  Rest   A       
#> 4  9.73 11.9  Rest   B       
#> 5 13.1   9.03 Rest   A       
#> 6  9.96  3.64 Rest   B

processed_recipe <- recipe(class ~ ., data = circle_example2) %>%
  step_dummy(category)

prepped <- prep(processed_recipe)

prep(prepped, training = circle_example2, fresh = FALSE)
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          3
#> 
#> Training data contained 400 data points and no missing data.
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Dummy variables from category [trained]

prep(prepped, training = circle_example2, fresh = TRUE)
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `category` doesn't exist.
```

The problem is with `processed$term_info`, which looks like this after the first `prep()` call:

```r
prepped$term_info
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   variable   type    role      source  
#>   <chr>      <chr>   <chr>     <chr>   
#> 1 x          numeric predictor original
#> 2 y          numeric predictor original
#> 3 class      nominal outcome   original
#> 4 category_B numeric predictor derived
```

Notice that there isn't a `category` variable here, it has been processed into `category_B` by the `step_dummy()` call. When `prep(fresh = TRUE)` is called later on, it will still use this processed term_info, so when it tries to look up the `category` variable using the tidyselect selection in `step_dummy(category)`, it fails because `category_B` is there instead.

title: Non-standard column names and step_dummy
description:
## The problem

Non-standard variables names are not supported by `step`* functions. The problem is caused by the use of `str2lang`. I don't quite see where str2lang is called, though.

## Reproducible example

```r
tibble(x=1:10,`variable b`=factor(sample(c('a','b','c'),10,T))) %>%
recipe(~.)%>% step_dummy(`variable b`) %>% prep %>% bake(NULL) 

tibble(x=1:10,`variable b`=factor(sample(c('a','b','c'),10,T))) %>%
  recipe(~.)%>% step_dummy('variable b') %>% prep %>% bake(NULL) 
```
Error:
```r
Error in str2lang(x) : <text>:1:11: unexpected symbol
1: ~variable b
```

title: `skip = TRUE` is not the default for `step_naomit`.
description:
Hello, this commit https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/commit/108c14a59a83fe9978a5e633cee07dd8fff6d35a states that `step_filter()`, `step_slice()`, `step_sample()`, and `step_naomit()` will change their default to `skip = TRUE`. 

This resolves  a couple of different issues relating to predictions with these recipe steps: https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/pull/512#issuecomment-630215281.

However, the change was not applied to `step_naomit`:
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/5993319f73c4dd4ac5db0393a427106da230c56d/R/naomit.R#L25-L27

I wanted to see if this was an oversight. I would personally like to see `skip = TRUE` as the default for `step_naomit`.

Thanks for all the help!

title: Old recipe no longer performs the step_pca
description:
## The problem

I've found this problem you should probably be aware of:
Back in august 2021 I've created and saved a recipe with several steps, including the `step_pca`. I have been using the latest recipes package that was available at that time.

```r
rec_obj <- recipe(~ ., data) %>% 
  update_role(username, new_role = "sample ID") %>% 
  step_YeoJohnson(all_predictors()) %>% 
  step_center(all_predictors()) %>% 
  step_scale(all_predictors()) %>% 
  step_pca(all_predictors(), threshold = 0.65)

trained_rec <- prep(rec_obj, training = data)

saveRDS(trained_rec, "models/trained_rec.rds")
```
Since then, I've been using this saved recipe in scoring process for several months without any issues. Last month I've upgraded to the latest recipes version 0.2.0 and scoring no longer works:
```r
trained_rec <- readRDS("models/trained_rec.rds")

# baked data has the same number of variables as data, all steps except step_pca seem to be executed
baked_data <- bake(trained_rec, new_data = data)
```
If I print `trained_rec `, I get the following:
```r
trained_rec

Recipe

Inputs:

      role #variables
 predictor        104
 sample ID          1

Training data contained 29546 data points and no missing data.

Operations:

Yeo-Johnson transformation on ... [trained]
Centering for ... [trained]
Scaling for ... [trained]
No PCA components were extracted from <none> [trained]
```
PCA step has somehow been lost.

## The solution
Downgrading the package version solves my problem:
```r
require(devtools)
install_version("recipes", version = "0.1.17", repos = "http://cran.us.r-project.org")
```

## Reproducible example
Sorry, but I can't (or don't know how to) write one since two versions of the recipe package are involved...

I'm using R version 4.0.4 on Windows.

title: Rename the step_normalize()
description: Please consider renaming the function `step_normalize()` to avoid confusion and misconception. `normalize` implies that we change the distribution of the variable (like what we do using Box-Cox transformation), however this function only standardize a variable (not changing the characteristics of a distribution). Based on what this function does, I believe `step_standardize()` would be a more appropriate name.

title: Variables vs Columns
description:

title: `step_dummy_multi_choice()` ignores levels of the input factor
description:
## The problem

`step_dummy_multi_choice()` ignores levels of the input factor and only considers levels in the new data. This causes problem if the downstream model uses a dummy variable for a level that does not occur in the new data. This behavior is in contrast to that of `step_dummy()`.

I also notice that the two functions have a common parameter called `levels`, and it looks like it is intended to explicitly specify the levels to include in the output. However, there are no examples in the documentation and I don't know how to specify (I tried `levels = list(x = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g"))` but it failed). Can you add some more explanations on how to use the parameter and/or add an example?

## Reproducible example

I would expect the following cases of `step_dummy()` and `step_dummy_multi_choice()` to produce the same number of columns. However, `step_dummy_multi_choice()` does not create columns for levels `"a", "b", "f", "g"`.

By the way, why do `step_dummy()` and `step_dummy_multi_choice()` produce different types of output (double vs integer)?

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(recipes))

# old data
tr <- data.frame(x = factor(c("a", "b", "c"), levels = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g")))

# new data
te <- data.frame(x = factor(c("c", "d", "e"), levels = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g")))

tr %>%
  recipe() |>
  step_dummy(x, one_hot = T) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = te)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>     x_a   x_b   x_c   x_d   x_e   x_f   x_g
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     0     0     1     0     0     0     0
#> 2     0     0     0     1     0     0     0
#> 3     0     0     0     0     1     0     0

tr |>
  recipe() |>
  step_dummy_multi_choice(x) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = te)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>     x_c   x_d   x_e
#>   <int> <int> <int>
#> 1     1     0     0
#> 2     0     1     0
#> 3     0     0     1
```

title: Condition `step_percentile()` on another feature, add `keep_original_cols` arg
description:
It would be great to have to the ability to condition the use of `step_percentile()` on another feature(s), and have the option to keep the output of the step using `keep_original_cols` which is present in many other step functions.

In the example below, the relationship between time and distance is bimodal, and I would like to filter out the observations that have a much higher distance to time relationship. This creates a much more accurate parameter estimate for the model.

``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(24)

race_data <- tibble(distance = sample(c(2,3,4), size = 1000, replace = T))

race_data <- 
  race_data |> 
  rowwise() |> 
  mutate(final_time = sample(c(rnorm(1, mean = 3, sd = 0.1) * distance,
                             rnorm(1, mean = 7, sd = 0.1) * distance),
                             1,
                             prob = c(0.95,0.05))
         )


# What would be awesome to do inside a reciepe
race_filtered <-
  race_data |> 
  group_by(distance) |> 
  mutate(percentile = ecdf(final_time)(final_time)) |> 
  filter(percentile < 0.90)


# Coefficent Estimate is skewed higher because of outlier points
lm(final_time ~ distance, data = race_data)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = final_time ~ distance, data = race_data)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)     distance  
#>      -0.394        3.352

# Coefficent Estimate is right on
lm(final_time ~ distance, data = race_filtered)
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = final_time ~ distance, data = race_filtered)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)     distance  
#>    -0.02693      2.99872


# An example of the how the API would work

race_rec <- 
  recipe(final_time ~ distance, data = race_data) |> 
  step_percentile(final_time | distance, keep_original_cols = T) |> 
  step_filter(final_time_percentile < 0.90)
```

title: Feature Request: Imputation
description:
I have been a big fan of tidymodels/tidyverse ever since I discovered them a few months ago. Yet when working with missing data, I have noticed that tidymodels (and recipes) have a few shortcomings. To quote from _[a certain staff blog from the University of Leicester](https://staffblogs.le.ac.uk/teachingr/2020/10/05/on-not-using-tidymodels/)_

> As an example, an important aspect of preparing the data for modelling is the replacement of missing data by imputation. So, tidymodels should have a design that helps us to make use of the many imputation packages already available in R. The problems of tidymodels imputation would exactly mirror those of broom. Lots of external functions offering different types of imputation, with the potential for more functions to be added in the future. So tidymodels needs to provide a framework for coding imputation.

I realize that this is more suitable for a milestone goal rather than a single issue. But if nothing, implementing a few recipe steps to call from [`mice`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/mice/versions/3.14.0/topics/mice) would at least spare many the trouble of having to separate missing-data preprocessing from the tidymodels pipeline. Thoughts or comments?

title: Potentially need a way to "unretain" a prepped recipe
description:
I.e. you might want to:

- prep a recipe with `retain = TRUE`
- use `juice()` to get the training data out
- do something with the juiced data (run a model)
- and then return a list where one of the objects is the prepped recipe. (for use in predictions)

What you _don't_ want to do is return the prepped recipe with the retained prepped training data. So it would be nice to be able to strip that off and then return the prepped recipe. Seems like we would need to do `object$template <- NULL` and `object$retained <- FALSE`

title: Feature suggestion: step_outliers
description: Even though `step_spatialsign()`, `step_BoxCox()` and `step_YeoJohnson()` can take care of outliers, it could be useful to have a step that handles them more directly. For example with Tukey's rule (Q1 − 1.5 * IQR, Q3 + 1.5 * IQR). The user could then have an option to remove them or replace the value with the cutoff or with NA.

title: Request `step_impute_random()`
description:
A recipe step that imputes using random values of the non-missing data. The way I see it, it is on the other side of the variance/bias tradeoff compared to `step_impute_mean()`. 

Bonus: this would work on all types of variables, not just numeric.

title: Random projection step
description:
I'd like a signature along the lines of:

```r
step_randomproj(recipe, ..., dimensions, error)
```

where the user can either specify the number of dimensions to project into or an acceptable level of error in the projection (then we could back out `dimension` from there).

It would also be nice be able to project into an arbitrary number of dimensions (i.e. also higher dimensions than the original data) to facilitate working with extreme learning machines or other random feature methods.

title: Prediction breaks when using step_select in recipe
description:
## The problem

I'm not 100% confident this is a bug... it might be intended behavior. I'm trying to use `step_select` in a recipe that I train and then later use to predict. For the workflow to function, I need to select the outcome variable so it can be passed through to the workflow. Later, if I try to generate prediction from a trained version of this workflow, I get an error upon prediction that the outcome variable does not exist. From some debugging I think this is because `workflow.predict` acts as if there is no outcome (which seems reasonable).

I think the preferred behavior is for `step_select` to always select the outcome variable in training and never try to select it during prediction. Not sure how hard this would be to implement. I also understand there are workarounds that use `step_rm` instead of `step_select`, but I think these are often suboptimal (eg. if I want to allow users to pass in dataframes of any shape). Reprex below.

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip

mod <-
  boost_tree() %>%
  set_engine("xgboost") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Training won't work if outcome is missing
rec <-
  recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_select(gear, carb)

wf <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec) %>%
  add_model(mod)

wf %>%
  fit(mtcars)
#> Error in setinfo.xgb.DMatrix(dmat, names(p), p[[1]]): The length of labels must equal to the number of rows in the input data

# If I select the outcome, workflow will train but fail to predict
rec <-
  recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_select(mpg, gear, carb)

wf <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec) %>%
  add_model(mod)

wf_trained <-
  wf %>%
  fit(mtcars)

wf_trained %>%
  predict(mtcars)
#> Error in `stop_subscript()`:
#> ! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `mpg` doesn't exist.
```

title: Package for handling outliers
description:
Hi @juliasilge and @topepo,

I have started to work on #850 (i.e. a package dedicated to handling outliers, *a la* `{themis}`). I have started to add a few common outlier handling approaches, but I wanted to get your thoughts on how outliers, once identified, should actually be handled. I see three main approaches:

1. **Set the outlier to missing**
     + This is perhaps the most straightforward solution. Just set the outlier value to `NA` which can be handled in later steps (e.g. `step_naomit()`, `step_impute_*()`, etc.).
2. **Set the outlier value to the threshold used for identifying the outlier**
    + For this approach, if we consider values beyond the 1st and 99th percentile as outliers, we could assign the 1st and 99th percentile values to the values beyond these thresholds.
3. **Remove/set missing the entire row**
    + This is sort of a special case when an algorithm is used not simply to find outlier values within a single variable, but rather identify entire rows/observations that are considered outliers based on sets of variables.
    + [`{lookout}`](https://sevvandi.github.io/lookout/index.html) would be an example of this scenario, where you use some set of numeric variables to identify outlier observations. Once an outlier is identified, should you **(A)** set the variables for the entire row as missing, **(2)** set the variables used in outlier detection for the entire row as missing, **(C)** remove the entire row from the data frame. 

From an API perspective, I thought maybe it makes sense to have an argument that controls this behaviour for every step, such as via a `method` argument:
```r
## Truncate at some computed thresholds (e.g. 99th percentile)
step_truncate <-
  function(
    recipe,
    ...,
    role = NA,
    trained = FALSE,
    thresholds = NULL,
    method = c('missing', 'replace', 'remove')
    na_rm = TRUE,
    skip = FALSE,
    id = rand_id('outlier')
  ) {
  ...
}
```

I look forward to hearing your thoughts.

title: Feature-wise tuning of common parameters
description:
Hi,

When adding `tune()` to recipe steps, such as for the `deg_free` parameter of `step_ns()`, the default tuning approach is to find the "best" value of `deg_free` (based on some metric) and that `deg_free` is applied to each variable. But it seems to be the more appropriate choice might be to find the best degrees of freedom for each variable independently, as there is often no reason to assume one `deg_free` is going to fit all. However, if I simulate 10 numeric predictors, where 8 have truly linear relationships and 2 are non-linear, the tuning will likely yield `deg_free` of `1` if the following recipe is used:

```r
recipe(Y ~ ., data) %>%
  step_ns(all_numeric_predictors(), deg_free = tune())
```

If I've got many variables that I want to explore non-linear relationships, it is quite verbose to type out each variable in its own step, e.g.:

```r
recipe(Y ~ ., data) %>%
  step_ns(X1, deg_free = tune('dfX1')) %>%
  step_ns(X2, deg_free = tune('dfX2')) %>%
  ...
  step_ns(X10, deg_free = tune('dfX10'))
```
Additionally, if I wanted to restrict each `deg_free` to a smaller set of possible non-linear transforms, I need to verbosely provide the `parameters()` object to `tune_grid()`
```r
  tune_grid(
    object = wflow,
    resamples = rs,
    param_info = parameters(
      dfX1 = deg_free(c(1, 3)),
      dfX2 = deg_free(c(1, 3)),
      ...,
      dfX10 = deg_free(c(1, 3)),
      mixture(), 
      penalty()
    )
  )
```

Is there a better way to allow for feature-wise tuning of a common parameter or is the manual approach shown above the only way?

title: Having a `translate_recipe()`  to print a recipe expressed as `dplyr`/`tidyr` code
description:
## Feature

The `step_*()` verbs are wrappers for preprocessing tasks. They convey clear meaning and standardize the procedure. However, they obscure the underlying code that is used to carry the procedure. Even if one digs inside the documentation and source code for what each step verb does, it is hard to comprehend what happens under the hood in a certain data set. 

Elsewhere, the `tidyverse` offers a possible solution to this. For example, consider [`show_query()`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/explain.html) from `dbplyr` that translates `dplyr` code to `SQL`. Similarly, [`show_query()` works in `dtplyr`](https://dtplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/translation.html) by translating `dplyr` code to `data.table` syntax.

I therefore wonder whether it's feasible to add a similar translation function to translate a recipe to `dplyr` and/or `tidyr` code. The advantage is mainly educational: users could _see_ the code and better _understand_ what is going on under the hood. They may have insights about it, and consequently ideas to improve it or write new `step_*()` verbs that address a preprocessing task slightly differently. 

For example, [this StackOverflow post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/70379233/how-to-translate-recipesstep-dummy-to-dplyr-tidyr-code) shows a desire to understand how `step_dummy()` works under the hood.

title: `prep(., retain = FALSE)` keeps record of dataset in `environment(steps[[i]]$terms[[j]])[["."]]$template`
description:
According to the docs, `prep(., retain = FALSE)` should _not_ keep the original dataset in the object, causing a smaller object size.
However, the training dataset is only removed from the template slot.
Each step keeps an additional copy in its `terms` environments, in `.$template`.

To see the problem, follow below reprex and see that we can greatly reduce the size, by clearing the template slot of all term environments in the recipe - all while still allowing `bake` to succeed.

This behaviour is particularly problematic when using recipes with large datasets, where it is necessary to strip as much data from the trained recipe as possible for efficient production use.

I'm not certain that destroying the remaining data in `prep(., retain = FALSE)` won't break the original recipe, because the environments are the same. Therefor, if I am not mistaken, a correct fix would need to instead duplicate these terms and then create a new environment with the same parent before deleting the data.

I'm willing to work on a PR. Please let me know which approach you prefer regarding the modification of `environment(recipe$steps[[i]]$terms[[j]])`: in-place or copy?
In-place might affect code which `prep(., retain = FALSE)`'s and then modifies the recipe again to `prep()` a second time.

``` r
library(recipes)
library(pryr)

rec <- recipe(data = dplyr::bind_rows(rep(list(iris), 10)), formula = Species ~ .) %>%
  step_normalize(starts_with("Petal.")) %>%
  step_BoxCox(starts_with("Sepal."))

rec_prepped <- prep(rec)
rec_prepped_noretain <- prep(rec, retain = FALSE)
rec_prepped_stripped <- prep(rec_prepped, retain = FALSE)

# even retain = FALSE keeps data

    step_normalize(starts_with("Petal.")) %>%
    step_BoxCox(starts_with("Sepal.")) %>%
    prep() %>%
    prep(retain = FALSE)
  lapply(r$steps, function(step) {

    prep = rec_prepped,
```

title: Helpers for groups/panel data
description:
Is there a way to apply one or more steps on a _per-group_ basis? Suppose we have panel data (surprise, surprise) and want to apply `step_lag` on each group, is there a trick to getting this to work now?

If not, I've got two ideas:
- add an argument to step template like `group` or `strata` that handles grouped-application in one spot
- add a step like `step_group()` or `step_stratify()` which acts like `dplyr::group_by()` in that following operations are applied per group. Would presumably then need `step_ungroup()`/`step_unstratify()` to revert to normal application. Might also be able to create a `group_by.recipe()` method, a `grouped_recipe` class, etc. to avoid new steps and use `group_by` very naturally?

From a UX perspective I'd lean towards the second; steps already have an awful lot of args, and mirroring `dplyr` would make this very easy on users.

title: Truncate a variable at quantiles of the variable distribution
description:
## Feature

I don't think a step like this currently exists, so I wanted to nominate `step_truncate` (could also be called `step_clip` or `step_clamp` maybe??):

The step would truncate numeric variables based on percentiles of the variable distribution. For example, if you wanted to truncate `x` at the 1st and 99th percentile, this would assign the 1st and 99th percentile value to observations that are below and above these values, respectively.

Perhaps a step already exists but I didn't see it. If there is interest, I can contribute a PR.

title: `step_hyperbolic()` add as a column
description:
### Tips for a helpful bug report: 

I think it would be useful if there could be a boolean for this to add columns as maybe an augment.

```r
library(tidymodels)

set.seed(313)
examples <- matrix(rnorm(40), ncol = 2)
examples <- as.data.frame(examples)

rec <- recipe(~ V1 + V2, data = examples)

cos_trans <- rec  %>%
    step_hyperbolic(all_numeric_predictors(),
                    func = "cos", inverse = FALSE, id = "cos")

cos_trans_b <- cos_trans %>%
    step_hyperbolic(all_numeric_predictors(),
                    func = "sin", inverse = FALSE, id = "sin")
```

The above will first perform a cos transform and then a sin of the cos, I think it would be useful to give the user the option to make these add columns as predictors. It is possible that a user may want the sin, cos, and tan of a value column to be future features.

title: Specifying `survival::Surv()` as the outcome in a recipe
description:
I am writing a modeling package and I wanted to include a recipe method for the primary modeling function. I ran into an issue when specifying the outcome in the `recipe()` function. It's a time to event outcome that is handled with `survival::Surv()`. The `recipe()` function returns an error, except when the `Surv()` object is evaluated before passing the `recipe()` (which is not the way a user would specify the outcome).

Any tips on how to add a recipe method for my modeling function?

Example below! Thank you! 

``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
library(survival)

# cannot specify Surv() on LHS
recipe(Surv(time, status) ~ ., data = lung)
#> Error: No in-line functions should be used here; use steps to define baking actions.

# can specify Surv() of LHS if evaluated before passing to `recipe()`
lung$surv_object <- with(lung, Surv(time, status))
recipe(surv_object ~ ., data = lung)
#> Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor         10
```

title: Enforce consistent PCA signs
description:
PCA rotations and scores are only unique up to their signs. One issue is that minor data modification might change the sign (examples in `?prcomp` actually says "signs are random"). This is sometimes hard to explain to new users. 

We can enforce a consistent sign by changing the sign of the entire eigenvector based on the sign of the first value of the eigenvector. In other words, 

```r
if (eigenvector[1] < 0) {
  eigenvector <- -eigenvector
}
```

The is done column-wise to the rotation matrix. 

This would only change the sign of the PCA scores for recipes that were prepped under this change (i.e., it is backward compatible).

title: recipe steps fail when running in parallel
description:
Hi! I ran into an issue when trying to fit resamples with a recipe using `bestNormalize::step_best_normalize()` & getting the error: `Error in UseMethod("prep"): no applicable method for 'prep' applied to an object of class "c('step_best_normalize', 'step')"`. I ran into [this issue from `tune`](https://github.com/tidymodels/tune/issues/192) suggesting that the error was due to running in parallel. When I ran sequentially, it worked! That issue (& the [recipes changelog](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/news/index.html)) mention that the issue should be resolved in recipes ver 0.1.15 - I have ver 0.1.16 installed,  so thought I might point out the potential existing bug!

 Here's a manual recreation of the error (it's pretty late as I'm writing this, so I didn't want to wait for reprex to eval):

```r
# splits & whatnot
diamonds_split <- initial_split(diamonds)
diamonds_train <- training(diamonds_split)
diamonds_test <- testing(diamonds_split)

diamonds_folds <- vfold_cv(diamonds_train)

# runs!
linear_mod <- 
  linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")

linear_rec <-
  recipe(price ~ ., data = diamonds_train) %>%
  bestNormalize::step_best_normalize(carat) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

linear_wf <-
  workflow() %>%
  add_model(linear_mod) %>%
  add_recipe(linear_rec)

linear_rs <-
  fit_resamples(
    linear_wf,
    diamonds_folds
  )

# fails!
doParallel::registerDoParallel()

linear_rs <-
  fit_resamples(
    linear_wf,
    diamonds_folds
  )
```

title: Move `master` branch to `main`
description:
The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). We anticipate this will happen by the end of September 2021.

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt

*message id: euphoric_snowdog*

title: `step_BoxCox()` possible speedup
description:
Identical FR as in #782 but for the BoxCox transformation. The [source](https://github.com/petersonR/bestNormalize/blob/master/R/boxcox.R) of the BoxCox function in the `{bestNormalize}`. 

```r
set.seed(123)
df = data.frame(x = rgamma(2e6, 1, 1))

f1 = function(x) {
  bestNormalize::boxcox(x, standardize = FALSE, lower = -5, upper = 5)
}

f2 = function(x) {
  estimates = recipes::prep(x, training = df, retain = TRUE)
  recipes::bake(estimates, new_data = NULL)
}

rec = recipes::recipe( ~ ., data = df)
rec = recipes::step_BoxCox(rec, x)

results = bench::mark(
  iterations = 10, check = FALSE,
  bestNormalize = f1(df$x),
  recipes = f2(rec)
)

results
#>   expression      min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr>    <bch> <bch:>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 bestNormalize 4.64s  4.78s     0.209     420MB     1.04
#> 2 recipes       5.94s  6.31s     0.166    1011MB     2.06
```

title: selecting no variables  in recipes selections in v0.1.15
steps that select no columns
description:
What should happen when the terms given by the user select no columns? This has come up a few times (see #140). 

The default, especially in the latest `dplyr`/`tidyselect`, is to fail. 

``` r
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(dplyr)

# dplyr: 
mtcars %>% select(torque)
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `torque` doesn't exist.

# recipes:
recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>% 
  step_center(torque) %>% 
  prep()
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `torque` doesn't exist.
```

<sup>Created on 2020-06-11 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

`recipes` has a different use case than `dplyr`: we may run filters that eliminate columns that we would have selected if they were there. In some cases, the selection is stochastic so it is not obvious about how to proceed. We want the step selection to be very robust and not break the recipe if this occurs. 

What would have to happen? I see three separate issues: 

## 1. between-step checks

It is possible that a step removes _all_ columns from the data. If that is the case, we should probably error out the recipe with an informative error message (the same is true for a zero-row outcome). 

This check would happen in `prep()`. 


## 2. within-step checks

For _each step type_, we could write code that looks to see if zero columns were selected and have this act accordingly during `prep()` and `bake()`. 

Using `step_medianimput()` as a test, I outlined how this should happen for this particular step (see commit 72b70ef7d). This is a simple step and others would be more complicated. 

The results: 

``` r
# devtools::install_github("tidymodels/recipes@no-selected-vars")
library(tidymodels)
#> ── Attaching packages ───────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels 0.1.0 ──
#> ✓ broom     0.5.6           ✓ recipes   0.1.12.9000
#> ✓ dials     0.0.7.9000      ✓ rsample   0.0.7      
#> ✓ dplyr     1.0.0           ✓ tibble    3.0.1      
#> ✓ ggplot2   3.3.1           ✓ tune      0.1.0.9000 
#> ✓ infer     0.5.1           ✓ workflows 0.1.1      
#> ✓ parsnip   0.1.1           ✓ yardstick 0.0.6      
#> ✓ purrr     0.3.4
#> ── Conflicts ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels_conflicts() ──
#> x purrr::discard() masks scales::discard()
#> x dplyr::filter()  masks stats::filter()
#> x dplyr::lag()     masks stats::lag()
#> x recipes::step()  masks stats::step()
data("credit_data", package = "modeldata")

## missing data per column
vapply(credit_data, function(x) mean(is.na(x)), c(num = 0))
#>       Status    Seniority         Home         Time          Age      Marital 
#> 0.0000000000 0.0000000000 0.0013471037 0.0000000000 0.0000000000 0.0002245173 
#>      Records          Job     Expenses       Income       Assets         Debt 
#> 0.0000000000 0.0004490346 0.0000000000 0.0855410867 0.0105523125 0.0040413112 
#>       Amount        Price 
#> 0.0000000000 0.0000000000

set.seed(342)
in_training <- sample(1:nrow(credit_data), 2000)

credit_tr <- credit_data[ in_training, ]
credit_te <- credit_data[-in_training, ]

# Does not work but should: 
recipe(Price ~ ., data = credit_tr) %>%
  step_medianimpute(Potato) %>% 
  prep()
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `Potato` doesn't exist.

# Does work:
rec <- 
  recipe(Price ~ ., data = credit_tr) %>%
  step_medianimpute(any_of("Potato")) %>% 
  prep()
#> Warning: `prep.step_medianimpute()` did not select any columns. This step will
#> not affect the data.

bake(rec, credit_te) %>% complete.cases() %>% mean()
#> [1] 0.906683
```

<sup>Created on 2020-06-11 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Some notes: 

 * We should really automate the warning message from within a handler used by `terms_select()`. The user shouldn't have to do this manually each time. 

 * Bare column names should be acceptable (i.e. the first example above with the unquoted `Potato`).

* The helper function `printer()` would need to be modified to show that no columns were selected. 

## 3. `terms_select()` changes

We do have a handler called `passover()` that is used by `step_dummy()` that does not throw an error when columns are not selected. It is likely that other changes are needed (e.g. the `strict` argument) to  `terms_select()` for this to work properly.

title: `step_YeoJohnson()` possible speedup
description:
I did a speed comparison of the Yeo-Johnson transformation functions from `{recipes}` and `{bestNormalize}` packages. It seems there is some overhead in `{recipes}` package (especially for large datasets) and I wonder if this can be optimized in some way.

```r
library("bestNormalize")
library("recipes")

set.seed(123)
df = data.frame(x = rgamma(20000000, 1, 1))

### bestNormalize
system.time({
  x1 = yeojohnson(df$x, standardize = FALSE, lower = -5, upper = 5)
})
#>  user  system elapsed 
#> 60.06    6.31   66.38
hist(x1[["x.t"]])

### recipes
rec = recipe( ~ ., data = df)
rec = step_YeoJohnson(rec, x)
system.time({
  estimates = prep(rec, training = df, retain = TRUE)
  x2 = bake(estimates, new_data = NULL)
})
#>  user  system elapsed 
#> 68.74   10.11   78.86
hist(x2[["x"]])
```

title: split up reference list of dummy variable steps
description:
the [STEP FUNCTIONS - DUMMY VARIABLES AND ENCODINGS](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/reference/index.html#section-step-functions-dummy-variables-and-encodings) reference page is getting a little crowded right now.

Both `step_date()` and `step_holiday()` could be their own section. Since they both deal with date variables.
 
Then I would suggest splitting the rest into the 3 main groups

- takes factor variables and return factor variables
- takes factor variables and return numeric variables
- conversion between different types

## factor2numeric steps

- `step_count()`
- `step_dummy()`
- `step_integer()`
- `step_ordinalscore()`
- `step_regex()`

## factor2factor steps

- `step_novel()`
- `step_other()`
- `step_relevel()`
- `step_unknown()`
- `step_unorder()`

## conversion steps

- `step_bin2factor()` numeric -> factor
- `step_factor2string()` factor -> string
- `step_string2factor()` string -> factor
- `step_num2factor()` numeric -> factor

At last, we have `step_indicate_na()`, which is an odd one out, and could fit a little bit everywhere. factor -> factor + numeric

title: Adding and offset option for 0s and 1s when using the step_logit()
description:
For logit transformation of values between 0 and 1, it may be a good idea to have an option to add/subtract a number (e.g., .0001) to 0s/1s to avoid -Inf/Inf.

This is something similar to the `offset` argument of step_log.

For instance,
```
step_logit(x, offset=0.0001)
```
first searches for 0s and 1s in variable `x` and adds/subtracts 0.0001, then applies the logit transformation.

title: Use of term "data recipe"
description:
The words "data recipe" are being used [3 times](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/search?q=%22data+recipe%22) in this package. Additionally, it is never used on https://tidymodels.org/ or https://juliasilge.com/

in the title of `prep()`

https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/433f2a8e589fb2875c1a07f6a6e49c7a251b16d1/R/recipe.R#L244

in the title of `bake()`

https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/433f2a8e589fb2875c1a07f6a6e49c7a251b16d1/R/recipe.R#L460

and as part of the `print.recipe()`

https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/433f2a8e589fb2875c1a07f6a6e49c7a251b16d1/R/recipe.R#L630-L632

I feel like it would be worth considering how often this phrase should be used. Either stop using it altogether to avoid potential confusion about what other types of recipes there are. Or expand the usage of the term across educational material.

title: step_date_cyclic(...) to feature code time into sin and cos
description:
*Updated: I initially proposed an API like `step_date(..., cyclic = TRUE)`. I now think that would be confusing because `features = "month"` would then mean "time of month" whereas it currently means "month of year". Instead, I propose a new function called `step_date_cyclic`*

## Feature
When forecasting, cyclical time-trends can be an important predictor. I propose to add a new function caled `step_date_cyclic` which feature codes `POSIXct` columns using trigonometric columns as `mlr3pipelines::PipeOpDateFeatures()`. E.g., for `features = "month"` it would add two columns: `sin(time)` and `cos(time)`. This avoids the data reduction inherent in the current categorical feature coding. And since many learners support numerical features, this enables more models to work on forecasting.

Here's one exposition of the rationale behind this feature coding: https://towardsdatascience.com/cyclical-features-encoding-its-about-time-ce23581845ca

## R code demo

Say the user has data with some timestamps:

```r
df = data.frame(
  timestamps = seq(as.POSIXct("2021-02-01"), as.POSIXct("2021-05-01"), length.out = 300)
)
```

Calling `step_date_cyclic(..., features = "month")`, would add two new columns:

```r
timestamps_secs = as.numeric(df$timestamps)
secs_per_month = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60
df$timestamps_month_sin = sin(timestamps_secs * 2 * pi / secs_per_month)
df$timestamps_month_cos = cos(timestamps_secs * 2 * pi / secs_per_month)
```

Visually:

```r
plot(feature_month_sin ~ timestamps, df)
points(feature_month_cos ~ timestamps, df, col = "red")
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1439417/116418263-42f83900-a83c-11eb-8043-587fd8d63481.png)


Jointly, these two columns uniquely identifies each time of month:

```r
plot(feature_month_cos ~ feature_month_sin, df)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1439417/116418394-628f6180-a83c-11eb-9ade-8af22dabe5a6.png)

## Postscript
For each `features`, two columns would be added. For each feature, just use `secs_per_{feature}`, and the rest should be the same.

title: `step_mutate()` shouldn't capture dots with `.named = TRUE`
description:
With `across()` in dplyr 1.0.0, it is becoming more common to have `mutate()` statements that don't have named dots. 

For example, I wanted to use `across()` to close this issue requesting `step_mutate_if()` #193, but the fact that we use `enquos(.named = TRUE)` keeps it from working right:

``` r
library(recipes)

df <- tibble(
  x = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  y = c(1, 2),
  z = c(TRUE, FALSE)
)

rec <- recipe(~., df) %>%
  step_mutate(across(where(is.logical), as.integer))

rec <- prep(rec, df)

bake(rec, new_data = NULL)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   x         y z     `across(where(is.logical), as.integer)`$x    $z
#>   <lgl> <dbl> <lgl>                                     <int> <int>
#> 1 TRUE      1 TRUE                                          1     1
#> 2 FALSE     2 FALSE                                         0     0


# Expected output
mutate(df, across(where(is.logical), as.integer))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       x     y     z
#>   <int> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1     1
#> 2     0     2     0
```

I think all we need to do is remove the `.named = TRUE` from this line:
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/254e7daa5e7d0448cd4be5fa54452ce30be362e7/R/mutate.R#L87

We should check other dplyr steps for this too

title: step_impute_mean per group
description:
## Feature

Currently, the way I see it, `step_impute_mean()` draws upon values from the entire column. There might be scenarios where it is more reasonable to impute missing values per group/subsample. I am aware that this could be easily achieved beforehand using `dplyr`, but I would find it much more elegant to have this option as part of the workflow - in particular, since then I am sure that my performance estimate is realisitic, since the mean was only computed on the training set!

I was thinking about something like
```R
recipe <- recipe %>%
  step_impute_mean(predictorA, group = predictorB)
```

title: Please expose eval_select_recipes

As far as I’m aware, users designing custom steps is supported, and this function seems critical to custom steps being able to select just some subset of the input data.

title: step_dummy renames dummy variable
description:
Below shows that I created a variable `dummyy` but with `step_dummy(all_nominal())`, it renames the variable to `dummyy_X1`. Although not shown below, this can create problems when original data and preprocessed data (through recipes) do not match on column names, especially when it's multiple dummy variables.

My guess is because `step_dummy()` creates multiple dummy variables when it is a multi level factor variable. However, it should not do anything in this case except convert it to numeric (though that could also be a concern, but I wouldn't know for all the modelling packages out there).

``` r
#rm(list=ls())
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
library(stacks)
library(baguette)
theme_set(theme_classic())

set.seed(123)

# Generate some data that increases over time
df <- data.frame(yearr = sample(2015:2021, 1000, replace = TRUE),
                 monthh = sample(1:12, 1000, replace = TRUE),
                 dayy = sample(1:29, 1000, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(datee = ymd(paste(yearr, monthh, dayy)),
         weekk = week(datee),
         yy  = sample(10000:20000, 1000, replace = TRUE) + (yearr^2) + (weekk^5),
         dummyy = as.factor(round(sample(0:1, 1000, replace = TRUE)))) |>
  filter(!is.na(datee)) |>
  arrange(-desc(datee))
#> Warning: 1 failed to parse.

folds = df |>
  sliding_period(lookback = Inf, # if Inf, then it's chain
                 period = 'week',
                 index = datee,
                 assess_stop = 1L, # include how many 'periods' in the future for training
                 every = 8L, # group how many 'periods' together
                 step = 2L, # how many 'periods' to move the window
                 skip = 8L) # skip how many first 'periods' for the model for assessment

#analysis(folds$splits[[1]])
```

title: step_geodist uses the Pythagorean theorem for latitude-longitude examples
description:
< -- ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ -->

## The problem

In `step_geodist` the Pythagorean theorem is used and the documentation examples use latitude-longitude pairs.  Unfortunately the Pythagorean theorem really doesn't apply to latitude-longitude pairs.  `step_geodist` returns the same distance for each example below, which is likely not what the user desires.  The Haversine function is one way to calculate the more common great circle distance.  

I can initiate a pull request with both options and a new `is_lat_lon` argument to `step_geodist` if interested.

## Reproducible example
``` r
library(pracma)   # for haversine function
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step

p1 <- data.frame(latitude = 88.0, longitude = 88.0)
ex_1 <- recipe( ~ ., data = p1) |>
  step_geodist(lat = latitude, lon = longitude,
               ref_lat = 89.0, ref_lon = 89.0) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)

p1 <- data.frame(latitude = 0.0, longitude = 0.0)
ex_2 <- recipe( ~ ., data = p1) |>
  step_geodist(lat = latitude, lon = longitude,
               ref_lat = 1.0, ref_lon = 1.0) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL)


ex_1$geo_dist
#> [1] 1.414214
ex_2$geo_dist
#> [1] 1.414214

pracma::haversine(c(88.0, 88.0), c(89.0, 89.0))
#> [1] 111.2288
pracma::haversine(c(0.0, 0.0), c(1.0, 1.0))
#> [1] 157.2494
```

title: persist local vairables used in recipe
description:
In situations when a local variable is used in a recipe (e.g. for cleaner code) that is not available during data processing, `bake()` will fail:

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dplyr'
#> Die folgenden Objekte sind maskiert von 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> Die folgenden Objekte sind maskiert von 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(recipes)
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'recipes'
#> Das folgende Objekt ist maskiert 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step


input<-data.frame(x=c("foo","bar"),y=c(1,2))
search_str<-"foo"
model_recipe <- recipe(y~.,data=input)%>%
  step_mutate_at(x,fn=
                   list(
                     bool=~grepl(search_str,.,fixed=TRUE)
                   )
  )
trained_recipe<-model_recipe%>%
  prep()

trained_recipe%>%
  bake(new_data=NULL)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   x         y x_bool
#>   <fct> <dbl> <lgl> 
#> 1 foo       1 TRUE  
#> 2 bar       2 FALSE

remove(search_str)

input_two<-data.frame(x=c("foo","bar"),y=c(1,2))

trained_recipe%>%
  bake(new_data=input_two)
#> Error: Problem with `mutate()` column `x_bool`.
#> ℹ `x_bool = (structure(function (..., .x = ..1, .y = ..2, . = ..1) ...`.
#> x Objekt 'search_str' nicht gefunden
```

I see no advantage in this flexibility as `recipies` is about consistency. Using local variables that may have different format or content during `prep` and `bake` may lead to undesired side-effects. Wouldn't it be better to 'codify' the variables' content in the _trained recipe_ for maximum transferability?

It may even be a new feature to offer variable injection during bake if desired.

title: An alternative to `tidy` for inspecting recipe with intuitive name
recipe_allows_novel_levels S3
description:
For tidymodels/workflows#112, we'll create an S3 method for steps and the recipe that indicates whether novel factor levels are handled in the step (and the recipe). Most steps will default to FALSE but `step_novel()`, `step_embed()`, `step_lencode*()`, `step_feature_hash()`, and others will be TRUE. 

The downside is that this will be a global declaration; most of these steps will be set up to deal with novel level from a specific set of predictors. It is possible that some other factor has novel levels and a failure results because the step isn't set up for that column.

title: `step_modeimpute` returns all NA when column is completely null, instead of mode from training data
description:
I'm not sure if this is intended behavior, or if I'm missing some other step that could help me to avoid this issue, but when using a recipe with `step_modeimpute` (this may also apply to other steps – didn't verify) on a factor column, when the column in `new_data` is completely NA, NAs are returned, as opposed to the mode from the training dataset.

```R
df <- data.frame(x = as.factor(c(0, 1, 0)))
binary_features <- 'x'

base_recipe <- recipes::recipe(df) %>%
	update_role(all_of(binary_features), new_role = 'predictor') %>%
	# Impute mode for binary features
	step_modeimpute(one_of(binary_features))

prepped_recipe <- prep(
	base_recipe,
	training = df,
	strings_as_factors = FALSE,
	retain = FALSE,
	fresh = TRUE
)
```

Let's try it out:

```
# Our original data.frame – looks good!
> bake(prepped_recipe, new_data = df)
# A tibble: 3 x 1
  x    
  <fct>
1 0    
2 1    
3 0    
# A new data.frame, with NA, 1, and 0 present. Still looks good – the mode is imputed.
> bake(prepped_recipe, new_data = data.frame(x = as.factor(c(NA, NA, 1, 0))))
# A tibble: 4 x 1
  x    
  <fct>
1 0    
2 0    
3 1    
4 0    
# Another data.frame, this time completely NA. No mode imputed.
> bake(prepped_recipe, new_data = data.frame(x = as.factor(c(NA, NA))))
# A tibble: 2 x 1
  x    
  <fct>
1 NA   
2 NA   
```

This behavior seems strange to me, but then again maybe I'm missing something and there's good reason for this.

title: Error when negation selectors are used in step_select()
description:
If you use a negated selection in `step_select()` then the remaining variables will be selected, including the response variable that could be missing later. Don't know if it should be fixed, but this is a case where the user should have used `step_rm()` instead. Maybe a note in the documentation will be enough.

``` r
library(recipes)
library(rsample)

set.seed(1234)
mtcars_split <- initial_split(mtcars)

mtcars_train <- training(mtcars_split)
mtcars_test <- testing(mtcars_split)
mtcars_test$mpg <- NULL

recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars_train) %>%
  step_select(-c(vs, hp)) %>%
  prep() %>%
  bake(new_data = mtcars_test)
#> Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.
#> x Column `mpg` doesn't exist.
```

title: Speed improvement for model.frame terms attributes
description:
## Feature

There are two calls to `model.frame` where the terms attributes are desired, one in dummy.R (`prep.step_dummy`) and one in misc.R (`get_rhs_vars`).  My understanding is that when only the term info is desired, you can do the model.frame on the first row and achieve equivalent results.  This will lead to improvements in processing time and memory consumption particularly for large datasets.  The following example shows that the term info is the same, but processing time and memory use are greatly reduced.  This likely will improve the performance of almost all recipes.  

``` r
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(bench)

n <- 5e6
nsub <- 5
set.seed(1)

dat <- tibble(
  num_col  = rnorm(n), 
  int_col  = sample.int(1:50, n, replace = TRUE),
  char_col = rep(paste('a', 1:nsub), each =n / nsub),
  fac_col  = factor(rep(paste('a', 1:nsub), each =n / nsub)),
  dt_col   = as.POSIXct('2010-01-01', tz = 'UTC') + 1:n)

form <- as.formula(num_col~.)

bench::mark(
  attr(model.frame(form, dat), 'terms'),
  attr(model.frame(form, dat[1,]), 'terms')
)
#> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is disabled.
#> # A tibble: 2 x 6
#>   expression                                     min  median `itr/sec` mem_alloc
#>   <bch:expr>                                 <bch:t> <bch:t>     <dbl> <bch:byt>
#> 1 attr(model.frame(form, dat), "terms")        616ms   616ms      1.62     903MB
#> 2 attr(model.frame(form, dat[1, ]), "terms")   357µs   370µs   2049.       126KB
#> # … with 1 more variable: gc/sec <dbl>
```

title: Bug: Using step_num2factor() to convert outcome to factor and change labels can only work with either fit_resamples() or predict() depending on skip = T
description:
## The problem

Trying to use `step_num2factor()` to convert an outcome in e.g. a logistic regression to a factor requires `skip = T` in order for `predict()` to work later on.
Also, if I want to simultaneously change the labels of the factor, then `predict()` will still work fine and `predict()` will simply use the new labels.
However, `fit_resamples()` cannot handle the fact that `skip = T` and the labels changed because then it cannot compute any metrics because it cannot compare the predicted class label to the "true" class

The following reprex is split into three parts:

1. **Base case:** `fit_resamples()` and `predict()` both work because the outcome was only converted to factor, the labels were not changed and `skip = T`
2. **fit_resamples problem:**   Base case is changed in the sense that outcome labels are now additionally changed from 0/1 to bla/blub. `predict()` still works fine because `skip=T` was not changed but `fit_resamples()` can still predict but not compare to "truth" because there will only be NAs
3. **predict error():** Additionally to case 2, now `skip = F`. Now, `fit_resamples()` can do both, i.e. predict and compare classification to truth, but `predict()` won't work anymore.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
set.seed(123)
fake_data <- 
  tibble(
    outcome = as.integer(round(runif(1000))),
    predictor = round(runif(1000, max = 2))
  )

fake_folds <- vfold_cv(fake_data, c = 5)


### Original labels simply converted to factor
fake_rec <-  
  recipe(data = fake_data, formula = outcome ~ predictor) %>% 
  step_num2factor(
    outcome,
    levels = c("0", "1"),
    transform = function(x) x + 1,
    skip = T
  ) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
fake_spec <- 
  logistic_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("glm")
fake_wf <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(fake_rec) %>% 
  add_model(fake_spec)

## This works because skip = T in step_num2factor()
fake_wf %>% 
  fit(data = fake_data) %>% 
  predict(new_data = fake_data) %>% 
  head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   .pred_class
#>   <fct>      
#> 1 0          
#> 2 0          
#> 3 1

## This works too 
fake_fits <- fake_wf %>% 
  fit_resamples(
    resamples = fake_folds, 
    control = control_resamples(save_pred = T)
  )
fake_fits$.predictions[[1]][1:3,]
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   .pred_0 .pred_1  .row .pred_class outcome .config             
#>     <dbl>   <dbl> <int> <fct>       <fct>   <chr>               
#> 1   0.458   0.542     3 1           0       Preprocessor1_Model1
#> 2   0.560   0.440     7 0           1       Preprocessor1_Model1
#> 3   0.458   0.542    15 1           0       Preprocessor1_Model1



############################
############################
############################
############################



### Labels converted to factor AND changed (with skip = T)
fake_rec <-  
  recipe(data = fake_data, formula = outcome ~ predictor) %>% 
  step_num2factor(
    outcome,
    levels = c("bla", "blub"),
    transform = function(x) x + 1,
    skip = T
  ) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

## This works because skip = T in step_num2factor()
fake_wf %>% 
  fit(data = fake_data) %>% 
  predict(new_data = fake_data) %>% 
  head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   .pred_class
#>   <fct>      
#> 1 0          
#> 2 0          
#> 3 1

fake_wf <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(fake_rec) %>% 
  add_model(fake_spec)


fake_fits <- fake_wf %>% 
  fit_resamples(
    resamples = fake_folds, 
    control = control_resamples(save_pred = T)
  )
#> ! Fold01: internal: No control observations were detected in `truth` with control ...
#> ! Fold02: internal: No control observations were detected in `truth` with control ...
#> ! Fold03: internal: No control observations were detected in `truth` with control ...

#> ! Fold10: internal: No control observations were detected in `truth` with control ...
## This does not work because of skip = T in step_num2factor()
## Nas in outcome and metrics cannot be computed

#>   .pred_bla .pred_blub  .row .pred_class outcome .config             
#>       <dbl>      <dbl> <int> <fct>       <fct>   <chr>

#> 2     0.560      0.440     7 bla         <NA>    Preprocessor1_Model1

fake_fits <- fake_wf %>%

## This does works because of skip = F in step_num2factor()

# But now this does not work
```

title: Bug: step_num2factor() cannot handle 0/1 numeric labels
description:
## The problem

`step_num2factor()` cannot deal with 0/1 numerical levels. `step_mutate()` plus `factor()` gets the job done though. Also, transforming labels such that they are labeled 3/4 works fine too. 

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip

## Labels other than 0/1 work fine
set.seed(123)
fake_data <- 
  tibble(
    outcome = round(runif(1000)) + 3,
    predictor = round(runif(1000, max = 2))
  )

recipe(formula = outcome ~ ., data = fake_data) %>% 
  step_num2factor(outcome, levels = c("0", "1")) %>% 
  prep()
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          1
#> 
#> Training data contained 1000 data points and no missing data.
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Factor variables from outcome [trained]


## 0/1 labels work only with step_mutate()
set.seed(123)
fake_data <- 
  tibble(
    outcome = round(runif(1000)),
    predictor = round(runif(1000, max = 2))
  )

recipe(formula = outcome ~ ., data = fake_data) %>% 
  step_mutate(outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("0", "1"))) %>% 
  prep()
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          1
#> 
#> Training data contained 1000 data points and no missing data.
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Variable mutation for outcome [trained]

## This fails
recipe(formula = outcome ~ ., data = fake_data) %>% 
  step_num2factor(outcome, levels = c("0", "1")) %>% 
  prep()
#> Error: Assigned data `map_df(...)` must be compatible with existing data.
#> x Existing data has 1000 rows.
#> x Assigned data has 493 rows.
#> i Only vectors of size 1 are recycled.
```

title: Generate warning for non-positive input to `step_BoxCox()`
description:
In the docs for `step_BoxCox()`, we say:

> The Box-Cox transformation, which requires a strictly positive variable, can be used to...

But when [a user tries to apply Box-Cox to non-positive input](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/67324077/step-boxcox-with-negative-data), it just silently doesn't do anything:

``` r
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step


set.seed(123)
n <- 2e3
x1 <- rpois(n, lambda = 5) # has some zero vals
x2 <- rnorm(n)             # has some negative vals
x3 <- x1 + 10              #  strictly positive
df <- tibble(x1, x2, x3)


rec <- recipe(~ ., data = df) %>% 
  step_BoxCox(all_predictors())

prep(rec)
```
