title: `step/update_*_if` scoped variants to be added?
description:
## Feature

I was wondering if it was possible to add some more scoped variants to the `recipes` functions. In particular `update_role_if` as a variant.

Sometimes in production code, I do not know if a particular `nominal` variable will have multiple levels or just a single level. If it has only one level, I'd like to update the role to `id`

``` r
library(recipes)

Plate1 <- data.frame(
  CopyNumber = log2(1e6/rep(c(5^c(1:4)), each = 5))/log2(1.7),
  Cp = runif(20, 5, 40),
  Dilution = rep(paste0(1,":",5^(1:4)), each = 5),
  Well = sprintf("W_%02d",1:20),
  Plate = "A"
)

rec <- recipe(CopyNumber ~ ., data = Plate1) %>%
  step_string2factor(all_nominal()) %>%
  update_role(Well, new_role = "id") %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

rec
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>         id          1
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          3
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Factor variables from all_nominal()
#> Dummy variables from all_nominal_predictors()

rec %>% prep()
#> Error: Only one factor level in Plate: A
```

Ideally there could be a `update_role_if` that could allow for a predicate to test

```r
rec2 <- recipe(CopyNumber ~ ., data = Plate1) %>%
  step_string2factor(all_nominal()) %>%
  update_role_if(all_nominal(), ~length(levels(.x))==1L, new_role = "id") %>%
  update_role(Well, new_role = "id") %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

rec2
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>         id          2
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          2
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Factor variables from all_nominal()
#> Roles updated from all_nominal() and ~length(levels(.x))==1L
#> Dummy variables from all_nominal_predictors()

rec2 %>% prep()
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>         id          2
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          2
#> 
#> Training data contained 40 data points and no missing data.
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Factor variables from Dilution, Well [trained]
#> Roles updated from Plate [trained]
#> Dummy variables from Dilution [trained]
```

In order for this to happen I imagine it might need to be recorded in the `$steps` of the recipe object. I haven't yet looked at what would be necessary in order to get this to work.

title: Mean encoding variables by fold
description:
Hi,
I'm playing a bit with the `recipes` and `rsample` packages and I would like to know if I'm using the packages correctly in the following scenario. The idea is to calculate the mean of a variable using just the train data of each fold.

Here is a reproducible example:

``` r
library(recipes)
library(rsample)
library(purrr)

# Load sample data
data("credit_data")

# Create folds
set.seed(55)
folds <- vfold_cv(credit_data, v = 3)

# Recipe
rec_obj <- recipe(Status ~ ., data = credit_data) %>% 
  step_center(all_numeric())

# Calculate means using training data and apply
# to all the data frame
calculate_means <- function(split) {
  
  # Calculate train means
  trn_mean <- 
    training(split) %>% 
    group_by(Job) %>% 
    summarise(Age_mean = mean(Age))
  
  # Modify split data
  split$data <- 
    split$data %>% 
    left_join(trn_mean, by = "Job")
  
  split
}

# Apply means (like prepper)
folds %>% 
  mutate(
    # 1) Add new features by fold
    splits_mean = map(splits, calculate_means),
    
    # 2) Apply pre-processing steps such as center, impute, PCA, etc.
    recipes = map(splits_mean, prepper, rec_obj, retain = TRUE)
    
    # 3) modeling...
  )

#> #  3-fold cross-validation 
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   splits            id    splits_mean       recipes     
#> * <list>            <chr> <list>            <list>      
#> 1 <split [3K/1.5K]> Fold1 <split [3K/1.5K]> <S3: recipe>
#> 2 <split [3K/1.5K]> Fold2 <split [3K/1.5K]> <S3: recipe>
#> 3 <split [3K/1.5K]> Fold3 <split [3K/1.5K]> <S3: recipe>
```

title: Loading the required packages for `step_nnmf()` makes `fit()` misbehave
description:
I was working on tidymodels/extratests#23 to move the tests for `step_nnmf()` out of recipes here (they are super long) when I noticed [some pretty strange errrors](https://github.com/tidymodels/extratests/runs/2272764312).

``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
data(biomass)

rec <- recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id var") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "split variable") %>%
  step_nnmf(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 2, seed = 473, num_run = 2) %>%
  prep(training = biomass)

linear_reg() %>% fit(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars)
#> Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable) : unable to find an inherited method for function 'fit' for signature '"linear_reg"'
```

<sup>Created on 2021-04-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

This error is happening because for some reasons `NMF::fit` is being called instead of `parsnip::fit`.

The required packages for this recipes step are loaded via `require()` within `prep()`, and once NMF is loaded, it seems to be causing some havoc:

https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/8152d8ec2419523f92b8217f09b99c70ec0744fe/R/nnmf.R#L150-L154

I am guessing from this that nobody has ever tried using this recipe step in a modeling context?

title: step_novel does not work properly with factors
description:
I recognize that this was raised as an issue (#627) and that in that example, the use of step_nzv() undid the effects of step_novel().    However, the solution provided by Julia simply demonstrated that step_nzv() should not be used after step_novel().  It did not address a more fundamental problem (at least it seems to me) with the use of step_novel() when a character variable is first transformed into a factor.   I am including the example from the documentation on step_novel() with one modification to demonstrate this issue.  I simply add step_string2factor() for diet before using step_novel() on diet.   This appears to result in the new levels of diet in test now set to NA rather than "new".   Am I missing something here?

library(dplyr)
library(recipes)
library(modeldata)

data(okc)

okc_tr <- okc[1:30000,]
okc_te <- okc[30001:30006,]
okc_te$diet[3] <- "cannibalism"
okc_te$diet[4] <- "vampirism"

rec <- recipe(~ diet, data = okc_tr) %>% 
  step_string2factor(diet) %>% 
  step_novel(diet)

rec <- prep(rec, training = okc_tr)

processed <- bake(rec, okc_te)
tibble(old = okc_te$diet, new = processed$diet)

Of course, this same code works fine if I simply remove step_string2factor() from the recipe

rec_2 <- recipe(~ diet, data = okc_tr) %>% 
  step_novel(diet)
rec_2 <- prep(rec_2, training = okc_tr)

processed_2 <- bake(rec_2, okc_te)
tibble(old = okc_te$diet, new = processed_2$diet)

title: Difficult to create an ordinal variable from character
description:
## Feature

I think it's difficult to create an ordinal variable from a character one. Here is an example:

``` r
library(data.table)
library(recipes)
library(magrittr)

foo <- data.table(bar = c(letters[1:3], NA))

rec_1 <-
    recipe(~., data = foo) %>%
    step_unknown(bar) %>%
    step_string2factor(bar, ordered = TRUE) %>%
    step_ordinalscore(bar)

bake(prep(rec_1), foo)
#> Error: Ordinal factor variables should be selected as inputs into this step.
```

The problem here is that `step_unknown()` converts the string variable `bar` to factor, thus, `step_string2factor` doesn't apply ordering. (This issue is already [mentioned here](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/311) but was closed unresolved.)

To me, the factor conversion that `step_unknown` does is not too intuitive and neither is `step_string2factor` skipping factors (thus ordering).

In the referenced issue it's mentioned that even if the character variable doesn't have any `NA`s and `step_unknown` is left out, one needs to use `string_as_factor = FALSE` in `prep`, otherwise the same thing happens. I don't mean to mix in too many different ideas here but think that these are related.

Maybe there is a better way of doing this but I didn't yet find it.

For the record, there are obvious workarounds (here is one) but not as elegant in my opinion:

``` r
rec_2 <-
    recipe(~., data = foo) %>%
    step_unknown(bar) %>%
    step_mutate(bar = factor(bar, levels = c("unknown", letters[1:3]), ordered = TRUE)) %>%
    step_ordinalscore(bar)

baz <- bake(prep(rec_2), foo)

baz$bar
#> [1] 2 3 4 1
```

title: Difficulties with naming in step_dummy()
description:
I'm opening this issue after a discussion in the tidymodels book club channel on slack:

I want to use the naming argument in step_dummy() in order to create dummy variables the same way  glm() and lm() functions de:  Instead of Species I want to have Speciesvirginica and Speciesversicolor as dummy variables.

The default of step_dummy uses the dummy_names() function as an argument, but I dont know how to modify sep parameter to be "' instead of "_". I was suggested to define a new function as a workaround:

```
library(recipes)
library(dplyr)
data(mtcars)

set.seed(123)

mtcars <- mtcars[complete.cases(mtcars),] %>%
  mutate(random_type = sample(c("a", "b"), nrow(.), replace = T))

nodash_names <- function(var, lvl, ordinal) {
  dummy_names(var = var, lvl = lvl, ordinal = ordinal, sep = "")
}

mtcars %>%
  recipe(~ gear + random_type, data = .) %>%
  step_num2factor(gear, levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5")) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), one_hot = T, naming = nodash_names) %>%
  prep(training = mtcars) %>%
  juice() %>%
  names()
```

If you'll run the code you'll see that it doesn't work well for numeric factors. 

@topepo  suggested that I'll use step_rename_at() as an alternative:

```
library(recipes)
library(dplyr)
data(mtcars)

set.seed(123)

mtcars <- mtcars[complete.cases(mtcars),] %>%
  mutate(random_type = sample(c("a", "b"), nrow(.), replace = T))


nodash_names <- function(var, lvl, ordinal) {
  dummy_names(var = var, lvl = lvl, ordinal = ordinal, sep = "")
}


mtcars %>%
  recipe(~ gear + random_type, data = .) %>%
  step_num2factor(gear, levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5")) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), one_hot = T, naming = nodash_names) %>%
  step_rename_at(everything(), fn = ~ gsub("X", "", ., fixed = TRUE)) %>%
  prep(training = mtcars) %>%
  juice() %>%
  names()
```

It works fine because I use sanke_case for columns names.

title: step_bs is extremely slow for large datasets
description:
In practice, especially for modelling tasks, datasets can contain a comparatively small amount of distinct values for predictors - even for continuous.

`splines::bs()` is very inefficient for such predictors, because it computes all basis functions for all rows separately.
This inefficiency is exacerbated by the fact that `recipes:::prep.step_bs` unnecessarily calls `splines::bs()` on the training data, throwing away the most expensive part of the computation altogether.

I have coded a small reprex with a fast preprocessing for `splines::bs()` that yields identical results for all aspects with one small exception: If `knots` is not provided and `df > degree`, the automatic knot selection algorithm for `splines::bs()` will select different knots if called with `unique(x)` instead of `x`.

As such, fixing the performance inefficiency in `recipes` is a little bit (but not much) more work than this proof of concept.

If there is interest in such a performance improvement, I can try coding up a pull request with more efficient versions of `prep.step_bs` and `bake.step_bs`.

### Minimal, runnable code:

``` r
library(recipes)
library(tibble)
set.seed(123)
v_u <- rnorm(100)
x <- tibble(
  v = sample(v_u, 1000000, TRUE)
)

t0 <- Sys.time()
rec <- recipe(x) %>%
  step_bs(v) %>%
  prep()

t1 <- Sys.time()
baked <- rec %>% bake(new_data = x)
t2 <- Sys.time()

bs_fast <- function(x, ...) {
  xu <- unique(x)
  ru <- splines::bs(xu, ...)
  res <- ru[match(x, xu), ]
  copy_attrs <- c("class", "degree", "knots", "Boundary.knots", "intercept")
  attributes(res)[copy_attrs] <- attributes(ru)[copy_attrs]
  res
}

t3 <- Sys.time()
baked_fast <- bs_fast(x$v) %>%
  unclass() %>%
  `attributes<-`(attributes(.)[c("dim", "dimnames")]) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  magrittr::set_colnames(sprintf("v_bs_%d", 1L:3L))
t4 <- Sys.time()

identical(baked, baked_fast)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(bs_fast(x$v), splines::bs(x$v))
#> [1] TRUE

cat(glue::glue(
  "prep recipe: {t1 - t0}\n",
  "bake recipe: {t2 - t1}\n",
  "total recipe: {t2 - t0}\n",
  "bake fast: {t4 - t3}"
))
#> prep recipe: 0.714876890182495
#> bake recipe: 0.235795021057129
#> total recipe: 0.950671911239624
#> bake fast: 0.11726713180542
```

title: The rentain flag in prep has weird behaviour
description:
## The problem

The retain flag in prep has weird behavior! The $template variable in the prepped recipe is never empty!
Either the retain flag is FALSE and the data from the recipe definition is passed, or the flag is TRUE and the data from the prep function is passed to $template. This is very unexpected as I would like to have no training data in case of retain = FALSE!

In the first possibility (retain = FALSE), 
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/d8858f8aedd10cfccb620c586d26c61632d0ea1d/R/recipe.R#L209-L216
the $template variable is filled during the recipe definition and not altered during the prep routine.
In case of retain = TRUE it is overriden when training data is specified.

https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/d8858f8aedd10cfccb620c586d26c61632d0ea1d/R/recipe.R#L479-L486

My expectation would be to change that code to 

``` r
if (retain) {
      if (verbose)
        cat("The retained training set is ~",
            format(object.size(training), units = "Mb", digits = 2),
            " in memory.\n\n")

      x$template <- training
    } else {
      x$template <- NULL
    }
``` 
For me this is important as I have a dataset of multiple GB which I don't want to keep for later, when I use the model! I'm happy to fix that and create a pull request if there is agreement on the fix.

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
    library(recipes)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
    
    train_mtcars <- mtcars %>% {do.call("rbind", replicate(10000, ., simplify = FALSE))}
    # Error if I dont specify a dataset here:
    mtcars_recipe <- recipe(mpg ~ hp + wt)
#> Error in form2args(formula, data, ...): argument "data" is missing, with no default
    
    mtcars_recipe <- recipe(mpg ~ hp + wt, data = train_mtcars)
    
    v1 <- prep(mtcars_recipe, retain = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
#> The retained training set is ~ 7.33 Mb  in memory.
    v2 <- prep(mtcars_recipe, retain = FALSE, verbose = TRUE)
    
    print(object.size(v1))
#> 7692800 bytes
    print(object.size(v2))
#> 7692800 bytes
    
    v1$retained <- NULL
    v2$retained <- NULL
    identical(v1,v2)
#> [1] TRUE
    
    # There is a difference if I pass a dataset explicitly to prep
    train_mtcars_2 <- train_mtcars %>% {do.call("rbind", replicate(2, ., simplify = FALSE))}
    
    mtcars_recipe <- recipe(mpg ~ hp + wt, data = train_mtcars_tibble)
#> Error in is_tibble(data): object 'train_mtcars_tibble' not found
    
    v1 <- prep(mtcars_recipe, training =  train_mtcars_2, retain = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
#> The retained training set is ~ 14.65 Mb  in memory.
    v2 <- prep(mtcars_recipe, training =  train_mtcars_2, retain = FALSE, verbose = TRUE)
    
    print(object.size(v1))
#> 15372800 bytes
    print(object.size(v2))
#> 7692800 bytes
```

title: referencing/using previous steps
description:
There are a variety of applications where it would be helpful for the current step to be able to reference the previous step (examples are #155 and [EmilHvitfeldt/textrecipes#3](https://github.com/EmilHvitfeldt/textrecipes/issues/3)). 

For example, if we center a column but want to uncenter it later, we would need the means from the previously executed `step_center`. 

The issue is in how the steps are executed. A simplified version of this is:

```r
for (i in seq(along = x$steps)) {
  if (!x$steps[[i]]$trained | fresh) {
    x$steps[[i]] <- prep(x$steps[[i]], training = training, info = x$term_info)
    training <- bake(x$steps[[i]], newdata = training)
  }
}
```

The most simplistic solution would be to pass _all of the previous_ steps to `prep` so that they can be referenced. Even with this access, there is no good way to refer to a previous step. The index could be used but is a poor choice. 

This thread is to start a discuss on how this can be solved in future versions that doesn't wreck objects created form the previous version.

title: Some thoughts on conceptualisation
description:
#### Vocabulary

- "Meal". I think the recipe analogy should not be pushed too far. E.g. stuff like "meal" or "serving the meal" become (perhaps paradoxically) abstract because too remote from the concrete stuff that is represented. The analogy loses its functionality.

- "Actions". How about calling them verbs? The idea being that tidyverse DSLs have verbs, e.g. domain-specific functions that read like English. Examples of domains: data import, data tidying, plotting, modelling. Using "verbs" for each domain gives a lexical consistency to the tidyverse.

- "Feature": That's a specific term from machine learning and predictive modelling. It won't have meaning for many scientists. I think we'd be better off with a term that is both more generic and relevant to the tidyverse: variables or columns. When part of a model recipe, these become predictors. One variable can be involved in several predictors (e.g. interaction terms).


#### Verb nomenclature

Here are a few distinctions that I think would be useful. These terms do not have to appear to the end user but may help organise the functions provided in the modelling domain of the tidyverse:

 - Specification for data transformations (`data-recipes`) versus specification for aspects of the model (`model-recipes`). "Aspect" is used here as a general term. For classic modelling methods, that aspect is often a conditional expectation.

 - Verbs for applications of data-recipes to specific datasets (`data-process`), and verbs for transformations of model-recipes to operating data structures (`model-process`).

 - Interface for end users, and interface for modelling packages. In other terms user (`UI`) versus pkg (`API`). The model-process functions are typically part of the API.


##### Standardisation

→ UI, data-recipe

Applies to a column and to a set of columns. We discussed with Hadley the issue of functions that apply to both vectors and lists/tibbles. This issue comes up in Tidyr and we don't have a solution yet.


##### Imputation

→ UI, data-recipe *and* model-recipe

- Defines a model within a model.
- Typically increases the dimensionality of the data (Rubin's method) in which case we end up with several datasets.
- But not always: some imputation procedures have a trivial model and do not account for variability. These procedures yield a scalar replacement (e.g. replace missing values with the mean)


##### Subsampling

→ UI, data-recipe

Should it be framed in terms of increasing the dimensionality of the dataset rather than adding/substracting rows? E.g. create bootstrap replicates, or partition the data in training/testing sets. We get multiple datasets.


##### Univariate transformation

→ UI, data-recipe

- Continuous-continuous: log, box-cox etc.
- Continuous-discrete: binning


##### Multivariate summarisation

→ UI, data-recipe

- Continuous-continous: PCA
- Discrete-continuous: correspondence analysis

Defines a many-to-one transformation of dataframe columns. This should not be compared with producing dummy variables (e.g. a one-to-many transformation) because the latter is a model-process API rather than a data-recipe UI.

The `gather` keyword from tidyr may be relevant here (and `spread` for a one-to-many transformation).


##### Interaction

→ UI, model-recipe / API, model-process

This applies to the specification of a model aspect. One possible effect of such a specification is to transform the data to a design matrix (API, model-process verb).


##### Dummy variables

→ API, model-process

Contrarily to interactions, this shouldn't come up in the UI. This will be useful to power users only in specific cases, e.g.  transforming data before a Jags analysis. This is normally used for creating design matrices.

In other words, the list of terms and their state may change as actions are taken

```r
sonar_rec <- Sonar %>%

```

Thank you again for all your work!

title: Documentation of feature engineering pipelines
description:
This is an incredibly interesting and exciting project. When I first saw it, one of the things that came to mind was usage of this software in regulated industries and how it could solve a whole class of problems.

Given your example:

```
sonar_rec <- recipe(Class ~ ., data = Sonar) %>%
  step_center(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_scale(all_predictors())
```

I can imagine a feature where you can say `recipe(..., document="pipeline.html")` and it would then generate a document with something like:

1. A summary of the data that was passed in (number of columns, histograms of values, etc...)
2. A documentation of the pipeline steps that were taken with the step name, parameters about how that step was configured, and examples of before and after values from a sample (or a visualization of the change.)

So like:

-----------

# Feature engineering for the Sonar dataset

The Sonar dataset has N columns and M rows. The columns are as follows:

(some table about the columns)

(visualization about the coumns)

# Feature engineering steps

## Centering predictors

A centering step was taken on columns X, Y and Z. The previous mean was blah blah and the IQR was blah blah

## Scaling Predictors

A scaling step was taken on column s blah blah blah. The previous yadda yada was etc...

-------------

I hope that makes sense?

This could then be used as a baseline document for communicating the feature engineering steps in a modeling process or production pipeline. I am eager and excited to see how this work continues!

title: step_dummy returns less binary variables if a character is provided with less categories
description:
Thank you for the package, I find it very useful! 

I found an unexpected behaviour when applying `bake` with a `step_dummy` recipe in a test dataset that have less categories in a character variable. In this case, `bake` doesn't return a binary variable for the missing category.

I attach a reproducible example.

```{R}
library("recipes")
library("dplyr")

data(okc)
okc <- okc[complete.cases(okc),]

rec <- recipe(~ diet, data = okc)

dummies <- rec %>% step_dummy(diet)
dummies <- prep(dummies, training = okc)

dummy_data <- bake(dummies, newdata = okc)

# [17] "diet_vegetarian"   

# Remove one category in diet
dummy_data <- bake(dummies, newdata = okc %>% filter(diet != 'halal'))

names(dummy_data)
```

title: New Function: train_test_split
description:
Feature Request: New function to efficiently split data into training, test and validations sets. 

This is a super common action, and recipes seems like a good package for it:
- python / sklearn.model_selection has `train_test_split()`
- H2O for R has `h2o.splitFrame()` (I love this function, but is for H2OFrame objects, not tidy df's)

Here's a potential version called `train_test_split()` that I'm using currently in the tidyverse. Still needs some work for handling errors and incorrect inputs. You might be able to use it as a start. The important thing is to drive the split by the `ratios` argument (same as `h2o.splitFrame()`). One ratio splits into train and test. Two ratios splits into train, test, and validation sets. 

``` r
train_test_split <- function(data, ratios = 0.7, seed = NULL) {
  
  # Checks
  if (sum(ratios) > 1) stop("`ratios` must be less than 1")
  if (sum(ratios) < 0) stop("`ratios` must be greater than 0")
  if (length(ratios) > 2 || length(ratios) < 0) stop("`ratios` must be one or two in length")
  if (!is.numeric(ratios)) stop("`ratios` must be numeric")
  
  n_row <- nrow(data)
  
  # Create splitting specification
  if (length(ratios) == 1) {
      spec <- c(train = ratios[[1]], test = 1 - sum(ratios))
  } else if(length(ratios) == 2) {
    spec <- c(train = ratios[[1]], test = ratios[[2]], valid = 1 - sum(ratios))
  } else {
    stop("`ratios` must be length 1 or 2")
  }
  
  # Create splitter
  if(!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  splitter <- sample(cut(seq(n_row), n_row * cumsum(c(0, spec)), labels = names(spec)))
  
  # Split using splitter
  ret <- split(data, splitter)
  
  return(ret)
  
}
```

title: Errors in many `bake` methods when `newdata` has class `grouped_df`
description:
Many `bake` methods will either raise an error or return an empty dataset if `newdata` is a grouped data frame (class`grouped_df` as returned by `dplyr::group_by`).  The reproducible example below provides a few examples. This appears to affect any `bake` method which uses the pattern,
```
newdata <- cbind(newdata, ...)
```
The problem occurs because when `newdata` is `"grouped_df"` then this code will return a list rather than the expected data frame object.

Replacing instances of `cbind` with `dplyr::bind_cols` seems to solve the problem - it passes all tests and produces the desired results. I could submit a pull request, but I haven't fully grokked **recipes**, and I don't know if grouped data frames have other implications for recipes. Should groupings be removed? Have special treatment?

title: step_univariatefilter
description:
I'd like to add a `step_univariatefilter(rec, ..., role, trained, score, threshold, top_n)` that works like `caret::sbf` except in the preprocessing stage.

`score` would be a function that accepts a single predictor and a response and returns a value, say an OLS p-value. To begin, I'd imagine that when recipes have multiple outcomes the user will just have to select one of them.

If the user specified `threshold`, the step would select all features with a score above/below the threshold, and if the user specified `top_n` it would rank the features by scores and take the best `n` of them.

I think it would then be reasonable to provide some functions along the lines of `caret::anovaScore` and `caret::gamScore`, and I'd also like to provide functions to filter based on variance and OLS p-values.

I'd imagine using variance/OLS p-value filtering for high dimensional data (Personally I'd like to do this for two genomics datasets with p > 16,000 and p > 420,000). If you have any advice re #88 in terms of making things fast, would love to hear it.

If this sounds useful, let me know and I'll submit a PR.

title: -long-double issues
description:
On 12/19/17: 

> This concerns packages 

> CBPS ExtDist GGIR RInSp RSQLite drtmle expss gamlss.inf lakemorpho lhs partitionComparison pre recipes tableone vpc xgboost xpose 

> which have 'noLD' 'Additional issues' reported on their CRAN results pages. And to quote the manual 

> <quote> Only test the accuracy of results if you have done a formal error analysis. Things such as checking that probabilities numerically sum to one are silly: numerical tests should always have a tolerance. That the tests on your platform achieve a particular tolerance says little about other platforms. R is configured by default to make use of long doubles where available, but they may not be available or be too slow for routine use. Most R platforms use ‘ix86’ or ‘x86_64’ CPUs: these use extended precision registers on some but not all of their FPU instructions. Thus the achieved precision can depend on the compiler version and optimization flags—our experience is that 32-bit builds tend to be less precise than 64-bit ones. But not all platforms use those CPUs, and not all which use them configure them to allow the use of extended precision. In particular, ARM CPUs do not (currently) have extended precision nor long doubles, and long double was 64-bit on HP/PA Linux. 

> If you must try to establish a tolerance empirically, configure and build R with --disable-long-double and use appropriate compiler flags (such as -ffloat-store and -fexcess-precision=standard for gcc, depending on the CPU type) to mitigate the effects of extended-precision calculations. 
</quote> 

> Packages partitionComparison and vpc do test for sums without a tolerance .... 

> Please submit a corrected update before Jan 24 to safely retain the package on CRAN. 

> -- 
> Brian D. Ripley, ripley@stats.ox.ac.uk 
> Emeritus Professor of Applied Statistics, University of Oxford

title: Feature Request: step_log1p

title: Safe to remove recipe$template?
description:
Hi Max, when a recipe is trained on a large dataset, we might not want to carry around a copy of it in the `template` slot. It seems like it's at least sometimes safe to delete it (code below seems to work fine). Do you have any guidance on when it might not be safe to? Thanks.

```r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({library(recipes); library(caret)})

data(segmentationData)
seg_train <- segmentationData %>% 
  filter(Case == "Train") %>% 
  select(-Case, -Cell)
seg_test  <- segmentationData %>% 
  filter(Case == "Test")  %>% 
  select(-Case, -Cell)

rec_obj <- 
  recipe(Class ~ ., data = seg_train) %>%
  step_center(all_predictors()) %>%
  step_scale(all_predictors()) %>%
  prep(training = seg_train)
rec_obj$template <- NULL
bake(rec_obj, seg_train)
bake(rec_obj, seg_test)
```

title: Coercion of characters to factors and values turned into NA
description:
Thanks for working on that package @topepo. I was surprised today about a character column getting coerced to a factor column. Here is a minimal reprex:
``` r
library(recipes)
library(dplyr)
mtcars <- tibble::as.tibble(mtcars) %>%
  mutate(letter = rep(letters, 5)[1:nrow(.)])
rec <- recipe(cyl ~ ., data = mtcars)
prep <- prep(rec, training = mtcars, retain = TRUE)
new_mtcars <- juice(prep)

class(mtcars$letter)
#> [1] "character"
class(new_mtcars$letter)
#> [1] "factor"
```

title: Reference level for bin2factor
description: Currently the level that replaces "1"s becomes the reference level. Is there a reason for that? My use case for this step is for outcomes, and there we definitely want whatever replaces "0" to be the reference level. If it were a predictor, I think you'd want the same... if you were getting a coefficient for it, you'd want the the change from no -> yes, but currently you'd get the opposite.

title: (generalized) linear embedding methods for categorical predictors
description:
Based on comments from topepo/FES#4 and topepo/FES#8, add recipes for taking the estimates of the coefficients in a `glm` or `stan_glmer` and use these to encode. 

Random thoughts:

* new levels would be encoded by the average of the estimates (at least that's how it would work in the Bayesian approach)
* use a `glm` and base `family` off of the outcome type (factor and numeric outcomes to start with). Not sure what to do about multinomial outcomes for now. 
* Fit a model for each predictor separately; including them all would raise the likelihood of linear dependencies and `NA` coefficient values. 
* maybe start a `stanrecipes` package to isolate that dependency
* `keras::layer_embedding` could be used to a [similar encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06737) and would probably lead to `tfrecipes`. We would have to convert the model output to `raw` to preserve the results after the session ends (unless we can get the coefficients and do it ourselves)

title: `step_scale()` not respecting prior dropped cols when run after a `prep()` step
description:
The following code removes a variable before a prep step. The `step_scale()` function ignores the fact that the column was previously dropped and output of the prep will show center step works on *3* cols, and scale on *4* cols (or in dev version says Sepal.Width is being scaled). Comment out the first `prep()` and the scale will show it's working on *3* columns. Very weird issue!

This is done in a single pipeline but represents the building of building different recipes in stages.

```
library(recipes)

iris %>% 
  recipe() %>% 
  step_rm(Sepal.Width) %>% 
  # comment out the next line to see the correct behaviour
  prep() %>% 
  step_center(all_numeric()) %>%
```

title: enable set.seed for any recipe steps that are not deterministic
description:
This is a cross-post from a [`caret` issue](https://github.com/topepo/caret/issues/928) that affects `recipes`.

Right now, `caret` preps a `recipe` twice: once to generate the dataset that `finalModel` is trained on, and, in a second step outside the `finalModel` training, it generates a second prepped recipe that is returned with the rest of the `train` output. The latter is what `caret` uses for transforming new data during later predictions out.

This means that any `recipes` steps that are not deterministic - I think the main cases that would affect users now are `step_upsample` and `step_downsample` - will lead to a caret `finalModel` that is not trained on the same dataset as the preprocessing recipe included for later. This is likely to be an invisible bug, except in cases where the difference between randomly-generated up/down-samples during the different recipe preparations becomes large enough to cause some downstream changes in (eg) which features are retained.

title: Upcoming `rlang` version is going to break sel2char()
description:
Using `rlang 0.2.2.9001`:

``` r
# from ?step_bagimpute
library(recipes)

data("credit_data")

set.seed(342)
in_training <- sample(1:nrow(credit_data), 2000)

credit_tr <- credit_data[ in_training, ]
credit_te <- credit_data[-in_training, ]
missing_examples <- c(14, 394, 565)

rec <- recipe(Price ~ ., data = credit_tr)

impute_rec <- rec %>%
  step_bagimpute(Status, Home, Marital, Job, Income, Assets, Debt)

tidy(impute_rec, number = 1)
#> Error: Can't cast a quosure to a character vector.
#> Please use `quo_text()` intead.
#> [90mCall `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace[39m
```

`tidy` calls `sel2char()` and that calls `as.character()` on each quosure term, which is no longer allowed. If the terms are _always_ quosures, then `as.character()` can just be replaced with `quo_text()`.

```r
> sel2char
function (x) 
{
    term_names <- lapply(x, as.character) #<- right here
    term_names <- vapply(term_names, function(x) x[-1], character(1))
    term_names
}
```

As of Sept 20th, 2018:
https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/commit/a44d34509461e388d2eaa3426e49b5d066894a9c#diff-569420c5f359608e35ac51fb3c5d0819R436

title: harmonize parameter names with `dials`
description:
It would be helpful to slowly harmonize recipe arguments that could be tuning parameters:

 - [x] `K` in `step_knnimpute` to `neighbors`. 
 - [x] `df` and `degree` in the spline steps; these need to be promoted to main args to the function
 - [x] standardize components in `step_pca`, `step_pls`, `step_isomap`, `step_kpca`, `step_ica` to use  `num_comp` (and `svm_sigma` for kPCA)
 - [x] add a `dials` parameter for threshold on [0,1]
 - [x] `step_bagimpute`: move `nbagg` out into a main option and name it `trees`. 
 - [x] `nunique` to `num_unique` in BC and TJ transformations
 - [x] `step_isomap` promote `knn` to main argument and rename



See if this can be done without breaking backward compatibility (maybe using the `...` to catch the old arguments and issue a warning).

title: Clarifying creation of interaction effects for categorical data
description:
There is an extensive [vignette for dummy variables and interactions](
https://tidymodels.github.io/recipes/articles/Dummies.html). However, it leaves out the explicit solution for creating interactions between categorical variables. Would you be open to adding this? E.g. by adding a modified example like this? 
``` r
library(recipes)
#> Lade nötiges Paket: dplyr
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'dplyr'

#> Lade nötiges Paket: broom
#> 
#> Attache Paket: 'recipes'

#> 
#>     step
mtcars <- as_tibble(datasets::mtcars) %>%
  mutate(gear = as.factor(gear), carb = as.factor(carb))

train <- mtcars[1:10,]
test <- mtcars[-c(1:10),]

rec <- recipe(~., data = train)

int_mod_1 <- rec %>%
  step_dummy(gear, carb) %>%
  step_interact(~starts_with("gear_X"):starts_with("carb_X"))


int_mod_1 <- prep(int_mod_1, training = train)

dat_1 <- bake(int_mod_1, test)
```

With recipes  0.1.3, my first approach was the above code, modified as follows:
```r
rec <- recipe(~., data = train)

int_mod_1 <- rec %>%
  step_interact(~starts_with("gear"):starts_with("carb"))
```

I.e. without creating dummies first, and that yields an error message difficult to digest:

In prep.step_interact(x$steps[[i]], training = training, info = x$term_info) :

Maybe the full example is too verbose and a sentence like: *To construct interactions between categorical variables, you need to convert all involved variables to dummy variables first* is sufficient, either in the warning message or in the vignette.

One issue is that the levels for the _original_ data are not stored. `rec$levels` contains the levels of the data once it is completely baked. So, we should:

1. Store the original levels in the same format as `rec$levels` (maybe called `rec$levels_orig`). This may include variables that don't exist later on (and/or have different levels or classes). 
1. Convert the current checking and conversion code to a function so that it can be run multiple times
1. Do the conversion right after the data are coerced to tibble but make sure that if `levels_orig` doesn't exist, don't fail.

title: `step_knnimpute` fails imputing numeric columns when other character columns are used for imputation
description:
`step_knnimpute` fails imputing numeric columns when other character columns rather than factor columns are used for imputation. Below are two minimal reproducible examples that illustrate instances where factor and character columns are used.

I have noticed that this fails on line 18 of `bake.step_knnimpute`. In the factor example, `new_data` will only have `fctr_col` where `object$ref_data` has the entire initial dataframe. In the character example (the step that fails), both `new_data` and `object$ref_data` will have all data from the initial df, but the `chr_col` is converted to factor in only `ref_data`.

``` r
library(recipes)
```

title: step_rm(skip=TRUE) not working with bake() leading predict() to fail
description:
The skip = TRUE argument of step_rm() doesn't seem to work with bake() as the variable still gets removed from the baked dataset. Additionally, the predict() function throws an error despite the fact that the removed variable isn't really needed in the model and the interaction that involved that variable, and is needed by the model, is available in the dataset to be predicted on.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(recipes)
library(caret)

rec_1 <- recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris) %>% 
  step_interact(terms = ~ Sepal.Length:Sepal.Width) %>% 
  step_rm(Sepal.Length, skip = TRUE)

train_ctrl <- trainControl(method = "none", classProbs = TRUE)

rf_1 <- train(rec_1, data=iris, method = "rf", trControl = train_ctrl)
#> Loading required namespace: randomForest

prep_rec <- prep(rec_1, iris, retain=TRUE)

iris_juiced <- juice(prep_rec)

iris_baked <- bake(prep_rec, newdata = iris)

colnames(iris_juiced)
#> [1] "Sepal.Width"                "Petal.Length"              
#> [3] "Petal.Width"                "Species"                   
#> [5] "Sepal.Length_x_Sepal.Width"

colnames(iris_baked)
#> [1] "Sepal.Width"                "Petal.Length"              
#> [3] "Petal.Width"                "Species"                   
#> [5] "Sepal.Length_x_Sepal.Width"

predict(rf_1, iris_juiced, type = "response")
#> Error in eval(predvars, data, env): object 'Sepal.Length' not found

predict(rf_1, iris_baked, type = "response")
#> Error in eval(predvars, data, env): object 'Sepal.Length' not found
```

title: Design question: keeping/deleting variables in steps at will
description:
In the future I plan on creating some steps that will extract information out of a variable (text listcolumn in textrecipes) and create new variables with them, much in the same way `step_pca` works. However I would like to be able to keep the original variables for later use.


So in this example `step_sentiment` would create a sentiment variable based on the text variable without deleting it as it is needed in `step_tfidf`. 
```r
okc_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = okc_text) %>%
  step_tokenize(text) %>%
  step_sentiment(text, keep_var = TRUE) %>%
  step_tfidf(text)
```

However in this example we would like  `step_sentiment` to create a sentiment variable and delete the text variable as it is no longer needed.

```r
okc_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = okc_text) %>%
  step_tokenize(text) %>%
  step_sentiment(text)
```

Is this something that you think should be supported within the recipe framework?

title: Feature request: Custom selector
description:
I have been trying to add a `all_textural()` function to match the `all_numeric()` and its cousins. However I run into the following road block:

``` r
library(recipes)
library(textrecipes)

data(okc_text)

okc_rec <- recipe(~ ., data = okc_text) %>%
  add_role(essay0, essay1, essay2, essay3, 
           new_role = "textual") %>%
  step_tokenize(all_textual()) %>%
  step_tf(all_textual())
#> Warning: Changing role(s) for essay0, essay1, essay2, essay3

prep(okc_rec, training = okc_text, retain = TRUE)
#> Error: Not all functions are allowed in step function selectors (e.g. `all_textual`). See ?selections.
```

<sup>Created on 2018-10-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Which seems to stem from the `element_check()` function. Would it be possible to allow for such change?

This issue is related to #221 as I would also need the ability to change/add the type of my columns which isn't (as far as I am aware) possible right now.

title: step_classdist() fails in creating new variable names when duplicate names exist (this was working previously)
description:
I updated all my existing R packages today and that seems to have broken the naming capabilities of the step_classdist() function for some reason. The below code previously added numbers to the newly created variable names if duplicates existed (until last night before I updated my R packages this morning). I tried uninstalling and installing both R and RStudio but it still doesn't work.

For the below example, previously, the first step_classdist() would create classdist_setosa and classdist_versicolor, the second step_classdist() would create classdist_setosa1 and classdist_versicolor1, the third step_classdist() would create classdist_setosa2 and classdist_versicolor2, and so on. But now, it throws an error:
 **Error: Name collision occured in `step_classdist`. 
The following variable names already exists: classdist_setosa, classdist_versicolor.**

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(recipes)
#>

iris_new$Species <- factor(iris_new$Species)

rec1 <- recipe(Species ~ ., data=iris_new) %>% 
  step_classdist(Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, class="Species") %>% 
  step_classdist(Sepal.Length, Petal.Length, class = "Species")

prepped_rec1 <- prep(rec1, training = iris_new, retain = TRUE)
```

title: Potential update.step() implementation
description:
For varying recipes parameters, we are going to need some way to update a recipes step. I have been using something like this for other "updating" purposes.

I think dials (or maybe a tuning package?) will eventually call something like this to merge a hyperparameter grid with a recipe, like dials can do with a model_spec and a param_grid.

``` r
library(parsnip)
library(recipes)

x <- recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris) %>%
  step_bs(Sepal.Length, degree = varying())

varying_args(x)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   name    varying id      type 
#>   <chr>   <lgl>   <chr>   <chr>
#> 1 degree  TRUE    step_bs step 
#> 2 options FALSE   step_bs step

update.step <- function(object, ...) {
  
  changes <- list(...)
  
  vctrs:::has_unique_names(changes)
  
  new_nms <- names(changes)
  old_nms <- names(object)
  
  for(nm in new_nms) {
    
    if (!(nm %in% old_nms)) {
      rlang::abort(glue::glue(
        "The step you are trying to update does not have the '{nm}' field."
      ))
    }
    
    object[[nm]] <- changes[[nm]]
  }
  
  subclass <- setdiff(class(object), "step")
  args <- unclass(object)
  
  step <- recipes:::step
  
  call_step <- rlang::call2("step", subclass = subclass, !!! args, .prefix = "")
  rlang::eval_tidy(call_step)
}

# update the varying field
update(x$steps[[1]], degree = 4)
#> $terms
#> <list_of<quosure>>

# fails
update(x$steps[[1]], degre = 4)

update(x$steps[[1]], deg_free = 5)
```

title: No formula and adding a step causes all variables to have role predictor role
description:
Hi,

Firstly, thank you for this wonderful package.

I have query regarding the behaviour of adding a step (example below uses step_dummy).  When I don't add a formula and perform juice(prepped object, all_predictors()), this returns all variables.  It seems by not having a role, then adding step it makes all variables have a role of predictor.  

Please see the examples below.  I've tried to illustrate the issue in the first one, with expected behaviour in the next two examples.  

Please excuse me if I've misused the package.  

Best wishes,

Oli

```r
library(recipes); 
library(nlme) # for data

# Add individual steps
obj_rec <- recipe(x = as.data.frame(Orthodont)) %>% 
  add_role(distance, new_role = 'outcome') %>%
  add_role(age, new_role = 'predictor') %>%
  add_role(Sex, new_role = 'predictor')  %>%
  step_dummy(Sex) 
obj_prep <- prep(obj_rec, training = Orthodont, retain = TRUE)
X <- juice(obj_prep, all_predictors()) 
head(X) # Expected?
y <- juice(obj_prep, all_outcomes()) 
head(y)

# No step_dummy
obj_rec <- recipe(x = as.data.frame(Orthodont)) %>% 
  add_role(distance, new_role = 'outcome') %>%
  add_role(age, new_role = 'predictor') %>%
  add_role(Sex, new_role = 'predictor') 
obj_prep <- prep(obj_rec, training = Orthodont, retain = TRUE)
X <- juice(obj_prep, all_predictors()) 
head(X)
y <- juice(obj_prep, all_outcomes()) 
head(y)


# Formula method works fine
obj_rec <- recipe(distance ~ age + Sex, data = as.data.frame(Orthodont)) %>% 
  step_dummy(Sex) 
obj_prep <- prep(obj_rec, training = Orthodont, retain = TRUE)
X <- juice(obj_prep, all_predictors()) 
head(X)
y <- juice(obj_prep, all_outcomes()) 
head(y)
```

title: step_upsample() in caret::train()
description:
When incorporating `step_upsample()` in a recipe and calling that recipe from `caret::train()`, the following occurs:

* Successfully able to train GLM model with Accuracy metric
* Not able to train GLM model with ROC metric; the outcome variable should have had 2 levels only
> Error: task 1 failed - "auc only works for binary outcomes at this time
* Not able to train RF model

> NA not permitted in response

### Minimal, reproducible example:

```r
library(recipes)
library(caret)
library(forcats)
data(okc)
okc$height[c(1, 34234,22322,2,22)] <- NA

rec_okc <- recipe(okc) %>%
    update_role(diet, height, new_role = "predictor") %>%
    update_role(Class, new_role = "outcome") %>%
    step_medianimpute(height) %>%
     step_mutate(diet = fct_explicit_na(diet, "missing")) %>%
    step_rm(-has_role("predictor"), -all_outcomes()) %>%
    step_upsample(Class, ratio = 0.5)


# WORKS:
okc_glm1 <- train(rec_okc, 
                 data = okc, 
                 method = "glm",
                 family = "binomial",
                 trControl =  trainControl(method = "cv", 
                    number = 3,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = defaultSummary, 
                     verboseIter = TRUE))

# Error: task 1 failed - "auc only works for binary outcomes at this time"
# this works if step_upsample() removed from recipe
okc_glm2 <- train(rec_okc, 
                 data = okc, 
                 method = "glm",
                 family = "binomial",
                 trControl =  trainControl(method = "cv", 
                     number = 3,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, 
                     verboseIter = TRUE),
                 metric = "ROC")
# Error: model fit failed for Fold09: mtry=2 Error in randomForest.default(x, y, mtry = param$mtry, ...) : 
#  NA not permitted in response 
okc_rf <- train(rec_okc, 
                 data = okc, 
                 method = "rf",
                 ntree = 500,
                 tuneLength = 5,
                 trControl =  trainControl(method = "cv", 
                    number = 5,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = defaultSummary, 
                     verboseIter = TRUE)
)

# Works
p_rec <- prep(rec_okc, okc, retain = TRUE)
dtrain <- juice(p_rec)
str(dtrain)
okc_rf <- train(Class ~ ., 
                 data = dtrain, 
                 method = "rf",
                 ntree = 100,
                 tuneLength = 2,
                 trControl =  trainControl(method = "cv", number = 2,
                     classProbs = TRUE,
                     summaryFunction = defaultSummary, 
                     verboseIter = TRUE)
)
```

title: Bake a recipe on only selected variables for Scoring Data (production)
description:
### Feature Request:

Use the `recipe` to do the pre-processing on production data (say scoring data) i.e., after finalizing a model with minimal number of variables. 
It would be ideal to be able to use the recipe only on a final set of variables, although the recipe was intended/prepped for all the variables. I do not see any such option in the current version.

Is it possible to introduce a new option (for example `optimize=TRUE` in `bake/prep` method ) to ignore and prep the data even if all variables not present during the baking? It will be handy when we start with many variables (say 200) but end up with a model using 15 variables. We do not want to create scoring data (production level) with all 200 variables.

For example, in the below scenario, I have prepared a recipe using formula method by including 5 variables. However, after modeling, I've finalized a model with only 3 variables. So considering I now have only 3 variables, when I try to bake on test data set with only these 3 variables, `bake` complains with an error. I understand, this is an intended behavior during the modeling process. However, would be helpful to ignore or be able to perform **bake** on only selected variables on a production level data after models are finalized.

This is some what similar to optimized **score code** generated by SAS which includes steps for variables that are present in the input(final) model. 

### Minimal, reproducible example:
```r
library(tidymodels)
#Training and Testing data sets creation
data(biomass)
biomass_tr <- biomass[biomass$dataset == "Training",]
biomass_te <- biomass[biomass$dataset == "Testing",]
```

```r
#Creating a simple recipe with step_center
rec <- recipe(HHV ~ carbon + hydrogen + oxygen + nitrogen + sulfur,data = biomass_tr) %>% 
  step_center(carbon,contains("gen"),-hydrogen)

#Prepping recipe using training dataset
center_obj <- prep(rec, training = biomass_tr)
center_obj
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>    outcome          1
#>  predictor          5
#> 
#> Training data contained 456 data points and no missing data.
#> 
#> Operations:
#> 
#> Centering for carbon, oxygen, nitrogen [trained]
#A simple linear regression model using only some of the variables
mymodel <- lm(HHV~carbon + hydrogen + oxygen,data=juice(center_obj))
mymodel
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = HHV ~ carbon + hydrogen + oxygen, data = juice(center_obj))
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#> (Intercept)       carbon     hydrogen       oxygen  
#>   18.063365     0.347025     0.206073     0.004804
#Creating test data using bake method prepped recipe including only variables from final model
transformed_test_data <- bake(center_obj, select(biomass_te,-nitrogen ,-sulfur)) 
#> Can't find column `nitrogen` in `.data`.
```

title: Recipes is 20 times slower than handmade pretreatment while training a caret model
description:
In order to build a stacking model, I trained many base models using different pretreatments on the same dataset. In order to keep track of the way to build the design matrices I used the recipes package and defined my own steps. But using a recipe with a custom step into a caret training model revealed to be 20x slower than applying the same pretreatment and training the caret model with the handmade design matrix. Any idea why and how to improve this?

Here is a reproducible example:
```
# Loading libraries
packs <- c("tidyverse", "caret", "e1071", "wavelets", "recipes")
InstIfNec<-function (pack) {
    if (!do.call(require,as.list(pack))) {
        do.call(install.packages,as.list(pack)) }
    do.call(require,as.list(pack)) }
lapply(packs, InstIfNec)

# Getting data
data(biomass)
biomass <- select(biomass,-dataset,-sample)

# Defining custom pretreatment algorithm
HaarTransform <- function(DF1) {
    w <- function(k) {
        s1 = dwt(k, filter = "haar")
        return (s1@V[[1]])
    }
    Smt = as.matrix(DF1)
    Smt = t(base::apply(Smt, 1, w))
    return (data.frame(Smt))
}

# Creating the custom step function
step_Haar_new <- function(terms, role, trained, skip, columns, id) {
    step(subclass = "Haar",  terms = terms, role = role, 
         trained = trained, skip = skip, columns = columns, id = id)
}

step_Haar<-function(recipe, ..., role="predictor", trained=FALSE, skip=FALSE,  
                    columns=NULL, id=rand_id("Harr")) {
    terms=ellipse_check(...)
    add_step(recipe, step_Haar_new(terms=terms, role=role, trained=trained, 
                               skip=skip, columns=columns, id=id))
}

prep.step_Haar <- function(x, training, info = NULL, ...) {
    col_names <- terms_select(terms = x$terms, info = info)
    step_Haar_new(terms = x$terms, role = x$role, trained = TRUE,
        skip = x$skip, columns = col_names, id = x$id)
}

bake.step_Haar <- function(object, new_data, ...) {
    predictors <- HaarTransform(dplyr::select(new_data, object$columns))
    new_data[, object$columns] <- NULL
    bind_cols(new_data, predictors)
}

# Fiting the caret model using recipe
system.time({
    Haar_recipe<-recipe(carbon ~ ., biomass) %>% 
        step_Haar(all_predictors()) 
    set.seed(1)
    fit <- caret::train(Haar_recipe, data = biomass, method = "svmLinear")  
})


# Fiting the caret model with hand made pretreatment
system.time({
    df<-HaarTransform(biomass[,-1])
    set.seed(1)
    fit2<-caret::train(x=df, y=biomass[, 1], method="svmLinear")
})

# Comparing results
fit; fit2
```
Both ways provides the same result but the recipes way take ~20 seconds while handmade pretreatment take ~1.5 seconds.
Using profvis, it looks like the recipe way made many attempts (i.e. 27 times) to do the same job using different runs of try() and eval() functions. Moreover the size of memory used is 10 times bigger.

title: Documentation of adding and updating a role
description:
Hi all, I had to update some older scripts today to follow the more strict role setting functions and I'm finding the documentation around `add_role()` and `update_role()` to be very confusing.

The documentation in [Manually Alter Roles](https://tidymodels.github.io/recipes/reference/roles.html) currently opens with

> `add_role()` adds a new role to an existing variable in the recipe. It does not overwrite old roles, as a single variable can have multiple roles.
>
> `update_role()` alters an existing role in the recipe.
>
> `remove_role()` eliminates a single existing role in the recipe.

Reading only these lines, I would confidently flip back to my source code and write

```r
recipe(mtcars) %>%
  add_role(wt, new_role = "predictor")
## Error: No role currently exists for column(s): 'wt'. 
## Please use `update_role()` instead.
```

Because I'd like to add a _new role to an existing variable_ (`wt`). Of course, this would throw an error because `update_role()` should be used to set the role for a column currently without roles.

I'm curious what problem is avoided by not allowing `add_role()` to set the initial role? Somewhat inline with [the discussion in this issue](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/283#issuecomment-459059467), I expected `add_role()` to, in essence, add roles to the "stack" of roles associated with a variable, in which case it makes sense intuitively (to me at least) that adding a role to an empty stack would initiate the stack.

Regardless, I have a couple constructive suggestions regarding the documentation that I believe would make it better align with the API.

1. Introducing `update_role()` first rather than `add_role()` would make it clearer which function to start with.
1. Indicate that `update_role()` can be used to initiate the first role of a column -- currently the focus on "alters existing role" makes it seem that `update_role()` is only relevant when a variable already has a role.
1. For `add_role()`, perhaps "additional role" instead of "new role" would better link with the _add_ verb (it seems natural when [used here](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/308#issuecomment-475697445)), and instead of "to an existing variable" I think "variables that already have a role..." would further clarify that a variable needs to have  role before `add_role()` is appropriate. I.e.
    
    > `add_role()` adds an additional role to variables that already have a role in the recipe."
1. Finally, in the Details section, I again recommend opening with `update_role()`.

    > `update_role()` should be used to replace an `old_role` with a `new_role` or when no role currently exists for a variable. `add_role()` only adds additional roles to variables that already have roles in the recipe and will throw an error when the current role is missing (i.e. `NA`).
    >
    > When using `add_role()`, if a variable is selected that already has the `new_role`, a warning is emitted and that variable is skipped so no duplicate roles are added.
    >
    > Adding or updating roles is a useful way to group certain variables...

If you're interested in the above, I'd be happy to prepare a PR if it would be helpful.

title: Feature Request: step_countByTermFreq() - Encoding Text Columns
description:
___Awesome Package___ - I use it, teach it, love it.

## Request
Make a version of `step_count()` that works with term frequencies instead of regex pattern matching. 

## Background
This is a common problem in spreadsheet data where you have a character field (e.g. Description Field) that has a product description that by itself has no value to the model, but when engineered (feature engineering) we can pull out various pieces that mean something and provide a ton of predictive value.

Here's an example. 

Product Description = "Synapse Hi-Mod Disc Dura-Ace Di2"

We can break apart this description into 5 Terms (5 columns) of Binary Flags (0/1) as to whether or not the terms occur in the Description.

One way to do this is with `step_count()` providing a regex matching `pattern = "Synapse"` each of the pieces. However, this manual process is not realistic, and there's a much easier way using term frequencies. 

 ## Feature Request & Example

The basic functionality I propose it to develop a function that uses a separator to split a text string into terms and uses the frequency of appearance to encode as binary flags. 

Here's a basic starting function.

```
step_countByTermFreq <- function(data, column, sep = " ", min_frequency = 4) {
    
    column_expr <- enquo(column)
    
    features_split_tbl <- data %>%
        select(!! column_expr) %>%
        separate(!! column_expr, into = str_c("Feature_", 1:1000), sep = sep, fill = "right") %>%
        mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
        select(row_id, everything())
    
    terms_tbl <- features_split_tbl %>%
        gather(key = "key", value = "term", -row_id) %>%
        filter(!is.na(term)) %>%
        mutate(term = term %>%
                   str_remove_all("[:punct:]") %>%
                   str_to_lower())
    
    term_frequency_tbl <- terms_tbl %>%
        select(term) %>%
        count(term) %>%
        arrange(desc(n)) 
    
    key_terms <- term_frequency_tbl %>%
        filter(n >= min_frequency) %>%
        pull(term)
    
    engineered_features_tbl <- terms_tbl %>%
        select(row_id, term) %>%
        filter(term %in% key_terms) %>%
        mutate(value = 1) %>%
        spread(key = term, value = value, fill = 0) 
    
    return(engineered_features_tbl)
    
}
```

With this function, I can quickly create flags based on how commonly the terms appear in the description field. Here's an example with a field "Model" that contains a product description. 

```
tibble(
    Model = c("Synapse Hi-Mod Disc Dura-Ace Di2", 
              "Synapse Hi-Mod Disc Red eTap", 
              "Synapse Hi-Mod Disc Dura-Ace",
              "Synapse Carbon Disc Ultegra Di2", 
              "Synapse Carbon Disc Ultegra SE")
) %>%
    step_countByTermFreq(Model, sep = " ", min_frequency = 1)
# A tibble: 5 x 11
  row_id carbon   di2  disc duraace  etap himod   red    se synapse ultegra
   <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1      1      0     1     1       1     0     1     0     0       1       0
2      2      0     0     1       0     1     1     1     0       1       0
3      3      0     0     1       1     0     1     0     0       1       0
4      4      1     1     1       0     0     0     0     0       1       1
5      5      1     0     1       0     0     0     0     1       1       1
```

We can then adjust the `min_frequency` if it's returning too many features. For most modeling applications we'd set this to 4 or more that way the term needs to appear at least 4 times to be encoded.

Let me know what you think.

-Matt

title: step_other reports that all the input columns have been othered
description:
### Minimal, reproducible example:

```r
data("credit_data")
rec <- recipe(credit_data, Age~Status + Marital + Home)
othered <- rec %>% step_other(all_predictors(), threshold=0.05, other="my_other") %>% 
    prep(training=credit_data)
othered
```

This will yield
> Operations:
> Collapsing factor levels for Status, Marital, Home [trained]

However, the variable _Status_ was not actually binned according to other, as it has only two values well above the threshold. Upon inspection of the steps, you will find that the variable Status has the attribute collapse = TRUE.
```r
othered$steps[[1]]$objects$Status
```
> $keep
> [1] "bad"  "good"
> 
> $collapse
> [1] TRUE
> 
> $other
> [1] "my_other"

Upon tracing through the code, I discovered the collapse flag is always set to true, when it should be dynamically evaluated.
```r
recipes:::keep_levels
```

```
function (x, prop = 0.1, other = "other") 
{
    if (!is.factor(x)) 
        x <- factor(x)
    xtab <- sort(table(x, useNA = "no"), decreasing = TRUE)/sum(!is.na(x))
    dropped <- which(xtab < prop)
    orig <- levels(x)
    if (length(dropped) > 0) 
        keepers <- names(xtab[-dropped])
    else keepers <- orig
    if (length(keepers) == 0) 
        keepers <- names(xtab)[which.max(xtab)]
    if (other %in% keepers) 
        stop("The level ", other, " is already a factor level that will be retained. ", 
            "Please choose a different value.", call. = FALSE)
    list(keep = orig[orig %in% keepers], collapse = TRUE, other = other)
}
```

The issue is in the last line of the function. Can we add in a collapse=all(orig %in% keepers) instead, or something similar?

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(recipes))

rec <- recipe(~ Sepal.Width, iris) %>%
  prep(iris)

juice(rec, all_predictors())
#> # A tibble: 150 x 1
#>    Sepal.Width
#>          <dbl>
#>  1         3.5
#>  2         3  
#>  3         3.2
#>  4         3.1
#>  5         3.6
#>  6         3.9
#>  7         3.4
#>  8         3.4
#>  9         2.9
#> 10         3.1
#> # … with 140 more rows

# should return tibble with 0 cols and 150 rows
juice(rec, all_outcomes())
#> Error: No variables or terms were selected.
```

If you look at `dplyr::select()`, a wrongly spelled column is an error, but a selector that returns 0 cols is fine.

``` r
dplyr::select(iris, "x")
#> Error: Unknown column `x`

dplyr::select(iris, dplyr::matches("x"))
#> data frame with 0 columns and 150 rows
```

`juice()` would still maintain the ability to error if someone did `juice(rec, non_existant_column)`.

I think we can get this behavior by simply removing the abort from `terms_select()` here:
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/master/R/selections.R#L196

That is a pretty commonly used function though, so maybe we'd want a version that is strict (the current behavior), and a version that isn't as strict (the suggested behavior).

```
library(tidymodels)
```

title: Predictions from caret train highly different from predictions from separate gbm model trained with the best tuned parameters when recipe is used
description:
I am tuning a gbm model and the preprocessing involves a recipe. I pass the recipe directly to caret's train function as recommend in the documentation for recipes. 

The best tuned model from train appears to perform fairly badly, while the gbm model trained with the best tuned parameters on the baked dataset performs much better. 

Why are the predictions from the two methods different? My understanding is that they should match, and in fact they do when I do not use recipes. See below for reproducible examples of each.

```{R}
library(DALEX)
library(caret)
library(gbm)
library(recipes)
library(tidyverse)
library(hydroGOF)

# sample the apartments dataset so runs are faster
set.seed(123)
df <- apartments %>% sample_n(500) 

# insert some NAs
df_preds <- as.data.frame(lapply(df %>% select(-m2.price), function(cc) cc[ sample(c(TRUE, NA), prob = c(0.85, 0.15), size = length(cc), replace = TRUE) ]))
df <- data.frame(df_preds, df$m2.price)
summary(df)

# define the seeds for each model
set.seed(123)
seeds <- vector(mode = "list", length = 6) ## length is = (n_repeats*nresampling)+1
for(i in 1:5) seeds[[i]] <- sample.int(n = 2000, 2) 
seeds[[6]] <- sample.int(2000, 1) ## for the last model
print(seeds)

# set up a tuning grid
grid <-  expand.grid(n.trees = c(500,1000), interaction.depth = c(2,4), shrinkage = 0.02, n.minobsinnode=10)

# define train control
fitControl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, seeds = seeds, repeats = 1, returnData = TRUE, verboseIter = FALSE)

# define a recipe with one step
train_recipe <- recipe(df.m2.price~., data = df) %>% 
  step_unknown(district)
train_recipe

# train the model with passing the recipe directly to train
tuner <- train(train_recipe, data = df,
               method = "gbm",
               bag.fraction = .5,
               distribution = "gaussian",
               metric = "RMSE",
               tuneGrid = grid, 
               trControl = fitControl,
               verbose = FALSE)
tuner$bestTune
tuner$results # models seem to perform badly

# predict with train model object
pred_train <- predict(tuner, df)
rmse(pred_train, df$df.m2.price)
plot(pred_train, df$df.m2.price)

# prep and bake the recipe to use in the gbm model
recipe_prep <- prep(train_recipe)
df_new <- bake(recipe_prep, df)

# create gbm model
set.seed(seeds[[6]])
bestr <-gbm(df.m2.price~.,data = df_new,
            distribution = "gaussian",
            n.trees = tuner$bestTune[[1]],
            interaction.depth = tuner$bestTune[[2]],
            shrinkage = tuner$bestTune[[3]],
            n.minobsinnode = tuner$bestTune[[4]],
            verbose = FALSE)

pred_gbm <- predict(bestr, df_new, n.trees = tuner$bestTune[[1]])
rmse(pred_gbm, df$df.m2.price) # gbm has a much better rmse
plot(pred_gbm, df$df.m2.price)

# the caret and the gbm predictions are highly different
plot(pred_train, pred_gbm)

#### Clear environment and train model without involving a recipe ####
# sample the apartments dataset so runs are faster
set.seed(123)
df <- apartments %>% sample_n(500) 

# insert some NAs
df_preds <- as.data.frame(lapply(df %>% select(-m2.price), function(cc) cc[ sample(c(TRUE, NA), prob = c(0.85, 0.15), size = length(cc), replace = TRUE) ]))
df <- data.frame(df_preds, df$m2.price)
summary(df)

# define the seeds for each model
set.seed(123)
seeds <- vector(mode = "list", length = 6) ## length is = (n_repeats*nresampling)+1
for(i in 1:5) seeds[[i]] <- sample.int(n = 2000, 2) 
seeds[[6]] <- sample.int(2000, 1) ## for the last model
print(seeds)

# set up a tuning grid
grid <-  expand.grid(n.trees = c(500,1000), interaction.depth = c(2,4), shrinkage = 0.02, n.minobsinnode=10)

# define train control
fitControl <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, seeds = seeds, repeats = 1, returnData = TRUE, verboseIter = FALSE)

# define response and data
train_data <- df[,-6]
train_response <- df$df.m2.price
                     
# train the model with passing the recipe directly to train
tuner <- train(x = train_data, y = train_response,
               method = "gbm",
               bag.fraction = .5,
               distribution = "gaussian",
               metric = "RMSE",
               tuneGrid = grid, 
               trControl = fitControl,
               verbose = FALSE)
tuner$bestTune
tuner$results # models perform much better than the above with recipe

# predict with train model object
pred_train <- predict(tuner, df)
rmse(pred_train, df$df.m2.price)
plot(pred_train, df$df.m2.price)

# create gbm model
set.seed(seeds[[6]])
bestr <-gbm(df.m2.price~.,data = df,
            distribution = "gaussian",
            n.trees = tuner$bestTune[[1]],
            interaction.depth = tuner$bestTune[[2]],
            shrinkage = tuner$bestTune[[3]],
            n.minobsinnode = tuner$bestTune[[4]],
            verbose = FALSE)

pred_gbm <- predict(bestr, df, n.trees = tuner$bestTune[[1]])
rmse(pred_gbm, df$df.m2.price) # gbm has a much better rmse
plot(pred_gbm, df$df.m2.price)

# the caret and the gbm predictions match
plot(pred_train, pred_gbm)
identical(pred_gbm, pred_train)
```

title: Error with dev tibble - problem with `strings2factors()`
description:

``` r
library(recipes)

trans_recipe <- 
  recipe(Species ~ ., data = iris)

prepped <- prep(trans_recipe, iris)

iris_no_outcome <- iris
iris_no_outcome["Species"] <- NULL

bake(prepped, iris_no_outcome)
#> Error: Tibble columns must have consistent lengths, only values of length one are recycled:
#> * Length 150: Existing data
#> * Length 0: Column `Species`
```

title: Create messages to prevent self-harm?
description:
Having chatted briefly about this at the Applied Machine Learning course in London, you thought it made sense for me to raise an issue on this point.

Specifically, given the opinionated nature of `recipes`, I wondered if you could create a warning or message in `tidymodels` (and, in particular, `recipes`) if a user seems to be on the verge of self-harm. For example, if they were about to use the test set when they should be using the training set. 

Whilst there might be more elegant ways, it could be done by scraping the string of the object name to see if it included (a variant of) the word 'test' in some way. 

I know that I'm paranoid about doing something like this by accident and I sense that I'm not alone on this.

Just thought it worth suggesting it as a possible idea.

title: new matrix classes for R 4.0.0
description:
Dear maintainer, 

Please see the problems shown on 
<https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_recipes.html>. 

Specifically, see the problems shown for the r-devel Debian checks. 

These can be reproduced by checking with --as-cran using current 
r-devel, which for now sets 
```
_R_CLASS_MATRIX_ARRAY_=true 
```
in the check environment, to the effect that 
```r
R> class(matrix(1 : 4, 2, 2)) 
[1] "matrix" "array" 
```
(and no longer just "matrix" as before). 

According to the R NEWS file, 

For now only active when environment variable _R_CLASS_MATRIX_ARRAY_ 
is set to non-empty, but planned to be the new unconditional behavior 
when R 4.0.0 is released: 

matrix objects now also inherit from class "array", namely, e.g., 
`class(diag(1))` is `c("matrix", "array")` which invalidates code 
assuming that l`ength(class(obj)) == 1`, an incorrect assumption that 
is less frequently fulfilled now. 

S3 methods for "array", i.e., `<someFun>.array()`, are now also 
dispatched for matrix objects. 

Apparently your package no longer works correctly when 
`class(matrix(...))` gives a vector of length two: please fix as 
necessary. 

See 
<https://developer.r-project.org/Blog/public/2019/11/09/when-you-think-class.-think-again/index.html> 
for more information about correctly using class() in package code. 

Please correct before 2019-12-18 to safely retain your package on CRAN.

title: bug with step_poly options argument

description:
If I use `step_mutate` the operations output is informative:
```
recipe(~ ., data = iris) %>%
  step_mutate(Sepal.Length = 1 / Sepal.Length,
              Petal.Length = 1 / Petal.Length) %>%
```

title: integer64 support
description:
There are cases where values of class integer64 from the bit64 package are treated as double without conversion. I noticed this with [`step_normalize`](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/1d3a89a982024c65176a0463f7b2e8bd3a0aa74a/R/normalize.R#L101), but it occurs elsewhere, for example in
 [`step_imputemean`](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/05c7410ee2c65d0cef77c015a64bf9bb9331e274/R/meanimpute.R#L103) and [`step_center`](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/e155bfb4a27f6c41fa393fbe26f9e23162ba2fe9/R/center.R#L107). In those cases the issue occurs because the `bit64::mean.integer64` generic returns integer64 and `vapply` expects a double.
```r
vapply(tibble(int_col=1:9, int64_col=as.integer64(1:9)), mean, c(mean = 0))
#>       int_col     int64_col 
#>  5.000000e+00 2.470328e-323 
```

If the package maintainers do not intend to support bit64, could we get a warning with these inputs?

### Minimal, reproducible example:

``` r
library(recipes)
data("credit_data")
rec_obj <- recipe(Status ~ Age, data = credit_data) %>%
  step_mutate(Age64 = bit64::as.integer64(Age)) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors())
trained_rec <- prep(rec_obj, training = credit_data)
train_data <- bake(trained_rec, new_data = credit_data)
train_data
```

title: `n_complete_rows()` should set names on `list_cols` before calling `map_dfc()`
description:
Prepping a recipe with a list column is a bit noisy with the development version of dplyr.

See the `New names` section? Those messages are always shown so its REALLY annoying in the tuning process.

``` r
library(recipes)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

packageVersion("dplyr")
#> [1] '0.8.99.9000'

x <- select(starwars, films, hair_color)

rec <- recipe(x) %>%
  update_role(films, new_role = "extra") %>%
  update_role(hair_color, new_role = "predictor")

prep(rec)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ...1
#> Data Recipe
#> 
#> Inputs:
#> 
#>       role #variables
#>      extra          1
#>  predictor          1
#> 
#> Training data contained 87 data points and 5 incomplete rows.
```

The issue is that in `n_complete_rows()` we call `map_dfc()` with just a character vector. I.e. `list_cols = c("films")`. If we name it, like `list_cols = c(films = "films")` then we won't get the notes. They come from `map_dfc()` calling `bind_cols()` which now uses `vec_cbind()` which is the noisy part.

Alternatively, I'm not even sure we need `map_dfc()` over just `map()`? I think you can assign a list into columns of a data frame like that?

```r
> recipes:::n_complete_rows
function (x) 
{
    list_cols <- purrr::map_lgl(x, is.list)
    list_cols <- names(list_cols)[list_cols]
    if (length(list_cols) > 0) {
        x[, list_cols] <- map_dfc(list_cols, convert_to_logical, 
            x = x)
    }
    sum(complete.cases(x))
}
```

I think we could literally just add 

```
names(list_cols) <- list_cols
```

description:
I'm prepping a dataset that has several numeric variables which I want to be treated as factors. The new behavior of `step_num2factor` requires the levels, which is fine, but now I'm not sure how to supply the levels for more than one column at a time. I tried to give it a list of character vectors, without success.
