title: formal argument "fresh" matched by multiple actual arguments
description:
I am following along in [Part 4 of AML](https://github.com/tidymodels/aml-training/blob/master/half%20day/Part_4.pdf). When I run `mutate(recipes = map(splits, prepper, recipe = ames_rec, fresh = TRUE))` I get the following error:

> Error in prep.recipe(recipe, training = rsample::analysis(split_obj),  : 
>   formal argument "fresh" matched by multiple actual arguments

I get the same error when running on my own example as well.

### Minimal, reproducible example:

#### Minimal, runnable code:
```
library(tidymodels)
library(AmesHousing)

ames <-
  make_ames() %>%
  dplyr::select(-matches("Qu"))
set.seed(4595)
data_split <- initial_split(ames, strata = "Sale_Price")
ames_train <- training(data_split)
ames_test  <- testing(data_split)
perf_metrics <- metric_set(rmse, rsq, ccc)

ames_rec <-
  recipe(Sale_Price ~ Bldg_Type + Neighborhood + Year_Built +
           Gr_Liv_Area + Full_Bath + Year_Sold + Lot_Area +
           Central_Air + Longitude + Latitude,
         data = ames_train) %>%
  step_log(Sale_Price, base = 10) %>%
  step_BoxCox(Lot_Area, Gr_Liv_Area) %>%
  step_other(Neighborhood, threshold = 0.05)  %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal()) %>%
  step_interact(~ starts_with("Central_Air"):Year_Built) %>%
  step_bs(Longitude, Latitude, options = list(df = 5))


set.seed(2453)
cv_splits <- vfold_cv(ames_train) #10-fold is default
cv_splits

cv_splits <-
  cv_splits %>%
  mutate(recipes = map(splits, prepper, recipe = ames_rec, fresh = TRUE))
cv_splits
```

title: Drop invariant variables
description:
I recently had to train many models, each for a subgroup. I built one recipe, which worked fine for all but a handful. They had a single value for on or more categoricals, which (rightly) broke `step_dummy`. It would be helpful to be able to drop invariant variables as part of the recipe. We could build a step for it, but it could also be part of `step_dummy`. I would say the former, so you can run it as a general function at the start of the recipe.

What do you think?

title: Proposal: step_relevel
description:
Is there any interest in adding a `step_relevel()` function? 

This could be valuable when creating model matrices with `contr.treatment` which takes the first level as the reference.

title: check_classes
description:
Description:
`prep.check_classes` will learn the classes of each of the colums.
`bake.check_classes` breaks when:
- column of which the class is learned is missing from `newdata`
- column is a of a different class than was learned in `prep`

Choices to make:
- do we consider `integer` and `numeric` as the same class? (I would say yes)
- do we consider `factor` and `character` as the same class? (I would say maybe add an argument for this that defaults to `TRUE`)
- do we allow for date time variables? (I would say yes).

title: Add ID interface to `tidy()` method for steps
description:
At rstudioconf, I got a question about extracting the information from an individual estimated step. For example, with box cox, maybe you wanted to know the exact value of lambda for the estimated step.

We could have a new verb that accepts a prepped recipe, and extracts the step information by `id` name. It would be as simple as `rec$steps[[1]]` for the first step (or a more specialized way that finds the right id name and returns that step).

I don't think we need to return the information in any special way, just return the list of info corresponding to that step, and let the user process it however they want.

description:
I came across this issue when trying to run glmnet model for classification and I'm unable to track the reason for this. Prepping the dataset proves that there are no Na before fitting the model. The issue seems to occur when while tuning the function is trying to make Cv predictions.

library(modeldata)
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(magrittr)

data("okc")
colnames(okc) <- tolower(names(okc))

okc <- sample_n(okc, 1000)

strata <- "class"
split <- initial_split(okc, prop = 0.8, strata = strata)

train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

cv <- vfold_cv(
  train,
  v = 5,
  repeats = 1,
  strata = strata
)

recipe_info <- train %>%
  recipe() %>%
  
  ### Roles assignment
  update_role(strata, new_role = "outcome") %>% 
  update_role(-one_of(strata), new_role = "predictors")

recipe_var_date <- summary(recipe_info) %>% 
  filter(type == "date") %>% 
  pull(variable)

recipe_var_numeric <- summary(recipe_info) %>% 
  filter(type == "numeric") %>% 
  pull(variable)
  
recipe <- recipe_info %>% 
  ### Imputation
  # Numeric predictors
  step_medianimpute(all_numeric(), all_predictors()) %>%
  
  # Categorical predictors
  step_modeimpute(all_nominal(), all_predictors()) %>%
  
  # Time predictors
  step_mutate_at(one_of(recipe_var_date), fn = as.factor) %>% 
  step_unknown(date) %>% 
  step_mutate_at(one_of(recipe_var_date), fn = as.Date) %>% 
  
  ### Handling time predictors
  step_date(one_of(recipe_var_date)) %>%
  step_holiday(one_of(recipe_var_date)) %>% 
  
  ### Individual transformations (optional)

  step_other(all_nominal(), all_predictors(), other = "infrequent") %>% 
  
  ### Dummyfying (optional features)
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors(), -all_outcomes()) %>% 
  
  ### Interactions (optional)
  
  ### Normalization (optional)
  step_normalize(one_of(recipe_var_numeric)) %>% 

  ### Multivariate transformations (optional)

  ### Removing unnecessary predictors
  step_rm(has_type("date"))

  ### Checks

# Check the structure of the input file
prep(recipe) %>% juice() %>% glimpse()

model <- logistic_reg(
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = tune()
  ) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

grid <- grid_max_entropy(
  penalty(),
  mixture(),
  size = 10,
  variogram_range = 1
)

workflow <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(recipe) %>%
  add_model(model)

tuning <- tune_grid(
  workflow,
  resamples = cv,
  grid = grid,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc),
  control = control_grid(verbose = TRUE)
)

title: Normalize vs Standardize - Naming Convention
description:
Hi @topepo & tidymodels crew,

Fantastic R package. It's a staple for me in all my preprocessing. Also love the new website. You guys are killing it!

## Question?

Should `step_normalize()` be renamed `step_standardize()` or have an option for scaling to the range [0,1]? 

My preference is to keep 1 function, but possibly add functionality to switch to the [0,1] range for those that expect a true normalization process. 

And, please let me know if I'm splitting hairs here, because "Standardization" (centering and scaling) is my preferred method (and thus I use `step_normalize()` for much of my numeric preprocessing routines. 

## Normalize vs Standardize Terminology

You can check out this [Stack Exchange article](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/10289/whats-the-difference-between-normalization-and-standardization) for details but basically the terms typically mean different things. 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13734662/80280277-0cd82480-86d1-11ea-9d96-9ad7ab840587.png)

- ___Normalization___ scales to range [0,1] 
- ___Standardization scales___ to mean 0, standard deviation 1 (preferred for preprocessing)

title: What's the best practice for modeling more than one outcome at a time?
description:
## The Problem

I frequently run projects for clients where I need to create multiple univariate models using the same features, but I have 10-20 different outcome variables. For example, maybe I'm modeling responses to survey questions with a consumer dataset as my feature space, and each question gets its own model.

Currently, the focus of `tidymodels` seems to be setting up a one-outcome variable recipe and then piping that into `parsnip` and possibly `tune`. I'm interested to know what the recommended way to handle more than one outcome variable at a time? 

My current workflow (reproduced below) is to create a list of recipes via map and then   construct a list of N recipes where the outcome variable changes. I can then map `tune_grid` over each recipe and then map `select_best` over all of those results. But, this feels over-engineered to me and not in the spirit of these tools.

So I ask if anyone has a better way to do this?

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(tidymodels)

sample_data <- tibble::tibble(
  binary_1  = rbinom(1000, 1, 0.7),
  binary_2  = rbinom(1000, 1, 0.55),
  binary_3  = rbinom(1000, 1, 0.30),
  feature_1 = rgamma(1000, 2, 1),
  feature_2 = rnorm(1000, 10, 20),
  feature_3 = rpois(1000, 5),
  feature_4 = rnorm(1000, 5, 15)
)

outcomes_vec <- sample_data %>%
  select(starts_with("binary")) %>%
  names()

sample_split <- initial_split(sample_data, prop = 0.8)

# Create a list of recipe objects, one outcome variable per recipe

recipes_list <- outcomes_vec %>%
  map(~ training(sample_split) %>%
    slice(0) %>%
    # Add all variables as predictors
    recipe(~ ., data = .) %>%
    # Update role for all outcome variables
    update_role(one_of(outcomes_vec), new_role = "extra") %>%
    # Specify which column(s) is/are the target/outcome for each recipe
    update_role(one_of(.x), new_role = "outcome") %>%
    # Remove the remaining outcomes
    step_rm(has_role(match = "extra")) %>%
    step_num2factor(all_outcomes(), 
                    levels = c("0", "1"), 
                    transform = function(x) x + 1) %>%
    step_center(all_predictors()) %>%
    step_scale(all_predictors())
)

title: Why does step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors()) process the target in classification?
description:
This [vignette](https://tidymodels.github.io/recipes/articles/Selecting_Variables.html) states that when working with dummy variables in a classification problem, using `step_dummy(all_nominal(), - all_outcomes())` should leave the target variable intact.

However, when trying to do the exact same thing the following way: `step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors())` it fails and needs to be changed to: `step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors(), -all_outcomes())`.

This behaviour is wrong right? In my mind the set of nominal + predictors should should return all nominal variables except for the target. 

I remember myself having to add `-all_outcomes()` many times in my different recipes when working on classification problems and wanting to preprocess categorical data, but all predictors and not the target. Using `all_nominal(), all_predictors()` should do the trick right?

### Minimal, reproducible example:

```r
library(modeldata)
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(magrittr)

data("okc")
colnames(okc) <- tolower(names(okc))

okc <- sample_n(okc, 1000)

strata <- "class"
split <- initial_split(okc, prop = 0.8, strata = strata)

train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

cv <- vfold_cv(
  train,
  v = 5,
  repeats = 1,
  strata = strata
)

recipe_info <- train %>%
  recipe() %>%
  
  ### Roles assignment
  update_role(strata, new_role = "outcome") %>% 
  update_role(-one_of(strata), new_role = "predictors")

recipe <- recipe_info %>%
  
  # Numeric predictors
  step_medianimpute(all_numeric(), all_predictors()) %>%
  step_BoxCox(all_numeric(), all_predictors()) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric(), all_predictors()) %>%
  
  # Categorical predictors
  step_modeimpute(all_nominal(), all_predictors()) %>% 
  
  # Time predictors
  step_date(date) %>% 
  step_rm(date) %>% 
  
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors())
```

A quick check below that proves that the outcome was processed as well:

```r
prep(recipe) %>% juice() %>% glimpse() %>% select(matches("class"))
```

```r
# A tibble: 801 x 1
   class_other
         <dbl>
 1           1
 2           1
 3           1
 4           1
 5           1
 6           1
 7           1
 8           1
 9           1
10           1
```

Only changing the last line to:

```r
step_dummy(all_nominal(), all_predictors(), -all_outcomes())
```

would fix the problem.

title: recipe saved to disk needs a lot of space
description:
I note that there are similar discussions, https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/301 and that `saveRDS` may save environments that are not visible in the size of the in-memory object with `object.size()`, e.g. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/30420598/r-rds-file-size-much-larger-than-object-size. I managed to isolate my problem in the below example. Space consumption of a recipe on disk saved from within a function seems to behave differently depending on:

- if huge objects are in the current environment. We can delete them and things are fine. However, from a practical point of view, the user should not have to do that himself and we often don't want to delete them beacuse they are used later.
- if the objects are saved from within a function. It seems that when creating the recipe in the global env, the problems don't occur.
- if there are any steps estimated. If there are no steps, huge objects don't seem to matter.


### Minimal, reproducible example:

``` r
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(dplyr)

data <- mtcars %>%
  dplyr::mutate(cat = letters[.data$cyl]) %>%
  slice(rep(1:nrow(mtcars), 1e5))

save_rec_in_fn <- function(data, rm_data = FALSE, step_string2factor = TRUE) {
  
  rec <- recipe(wt ~ ., data = dplyr::slice(data, integer()))
  if (step_string2factor) {
    rec <- rec %>%
      step_string2factor(recipes::all_nominal(), -recipes::all_outcomes())
  }
  if (rm_data) {
    rm(data)
  }
  saveRDS(rec, "rec")
  print("size of rec on disk: ")
  print(fs::file_size("rec"))
  
}

# keep data but no actual steps: fine
save_rec_in_fn(data, step_string2factor = FALSE)
#> [1] "size of rec on disk: "
#> 360
# keep data but string2factor step: not fine
save_rec_in_fn(data, step_string2factor = TRUE)
#> [1] "size of rec on disk: "
#> 2.57M
# remove data: always fine
save_rec_in_fn(data, rm_data = TRUE)
#> [1] "size of rec on disk: "
#> 792
save_rec_in_fn(data, rm_data = TRUE, step_string2factor = FALSE)
#> [1] "size of rec on disk: "
#> 360
```

title: Can you supply means/sds to the step_normalize/step_center/step_scale funs?
description:
Hi,

I am wondering if you can pass `means` or `sds` to the relevant step functions so that the centering and scaling is not estimated, but supplied. Maybe I am just doing it wrong, or perhaps this is not possible. I did look for other steps that would allow this sort of thing, but I didn't see anything that seemed appropriate. 

For example, if I wanted the centering to be `3`, rather than the arithmetic mean of `3.057`...I thought if I passed the named list with the centering value it would be used. `means` looks like an argument, but the description seems like it is only used internally when `prep`ing the recipe. Am I wrong about that?
```r
library(recipes)

rec <- recipe(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, data = iris)

mean_val <- list(Sepal.Width = 3)

rec_steps <-
  rec %>% 
  step_center(Sepal.Width, means = mean_val)

prep(rec_steps) %>% 
  tidy(number = 1)
```
Thanks for your help.

title: tidy tools for unsupervised learning methods?
description:
I discussed this Max during the Applied ML workshop at RStudioConf 2020, and he suggested that I opened an issue about it on this repo. 

I was wondering if there was any appetite in setting up tidy tools for unsupervised learning methods, particularly ensemble methods. The best package I can find on this is the [clue package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/clue/vignettes/clue.pdf). Unfortunately the only documentation about the package is the linked vignette, and I have found it unhelpful in understanding how the workflow is supposed to be implemented to apply a consensual ensemble clustering with a raw data set. 

This is tangentially related to #399, but I wanted at least to initiate a discuss whether there is an interest in going down that path. I often run clustering methods in my work, and I currently use a licensing software ([CCEA by Sawtooth Software](https://www.sawtoothsoftware.com/products/advanced-analytical-tools/ccea)). Being able to keep this work in the R ecosystem, particularly the tidyverse ecosystem, would be huge for me.

title: Wrong information displayed if one_of() used in step_rm()
description:
It seems like selection functions get only evaluated when `prep()` is called. That produces unexpected behavior when using `step_rm()` as showed in the following minimal example:

```
library(recipes)
library(tidyverse)

rec_test_data = tibble(response=1,x=1,y=1,z=1)
rec_test = recipe(response ~ ., data=rec_test_data)

remove = c("x")
rec_test = rec_test %>% step_rm(one_of(!!remove))

remove = c("y")
rec_test = rec_test %>% step_rm(one_of(remove))
rec_test

rec_test %>% prep(training=rec_test_data)
```

Output:

```
Data Recipe

Inputs:

      role #variables
   outcome          1
 predictor          3

Operations:

Delete terms one_of, x
Delete terms one_of, remove

Data Recipe

Inputs:

      role #variables
   outcome          1
 predictor          3

Training data contained 1 data points and no missing data.

Operations:

Variables removed x [trained]
Variables removed y [trained]
```

Looks like there were variables `one_of` and `remove` that will eventually get removed.

It seems to me like due to late evaluation there is no chance the printed recipe could show meaningful information about the variables that will be deleted in `step_rm`. The current output is misleading.

Second, I'm not entirely sure whether the following modified example (`!!` removed) should work or if the error thrown is reasonable. I would personally expect a different behavior, though it could be expected behavior in the tidyselect logic.

```
rec_test_data = tibble(response=1,x=1,y=1,z=1)
rec_test = recipe(response ~ ., data=rec_test_data)

remove = c("x")
rec_test = rec_test %>% step_rm(one_of(remove))

remove = c("y")
rec_test = rec_test %>% step_rm(one_of(remove))

rec_test %>% prep(training=rec_test_data)
```

Error thrown:

```
Error: No variables or terms were selected.
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.
In addition: Warning message:
Unknown columns: `y` 
```

Looks like `y` gets removed twice.

For me, it doesn't make sense to evaluate `remove` only when `prep()` is called since a character vector supplied to `one_of()` wouldn't typically be something dependent on the current dataset, but instead I understand `one_of()` and its similar versions to be a bridge to the surrounding scope with the purpose to enable passing external variables for selection.

```
sessioninfo::session_info()

title: `bake.step_holiday()` is noisy
description:
``` r
library(recipes, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- data.frame(x = as.Date("2019-01-01"), y = 1)

rec <- 
  recipe(y ~ x, data = df) %>% 
  step_holiday(x)

x <- prep(rec, df)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ...1
#> * `` -> ...2
#> * `` -> ...3
```

<sup>Created on 2020-05-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Right here we generate matrix column names with `""` and then coerce to tibble. In 3.0.0 of tibble this uses vctrs and is noisy.
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/2154f5d4e858db2a6eeb94378991ae996b395ed2/R/holiday.R#L146-L147

We should do like `bake.step_date()`, and generate the column names using a numeric sequence (the names dont really matter, they just have to exist)
https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/blob/2154f5d4e858db2a6eeb94378991ae996b395ed2/R/date.R#L218-L221

title: FeatureRequest:  A new step similar to step_rollimpute but with partition_by and order_by parameters.
description:
I'm not sure how roll impute works, but the documentation that it requires an odd numbered period around the point suggests that it applies the function over the future as well as past values.

One easy form of imputation would just be to take the last known value.  Or the average of the previous known values over a period of t.  But this would require two things, an order by variable (you have to know what is previous) and a partition by variable (you don't want to impute your first value as the last value of the previous subject, etc.).

I've already written an "impute last known value" custom step for my own work.  It doesn't use a custom function.  But I would volunteer to try to add this to the tidymodels universe.  I think a partitioned and ordered rolling impute would be quite useful.

title: R caret discretization within cross validation
description:
I'm using R caret package and I want to apply a discretization function to all predictive variables within cross-validation.

For example using this code:

```R
# load the library
library(caret)
# load the iris dataset
data(iris)
# define training control
train_control <- trainControl(method="cv", number=10)
# fix the parameters of the algorithm
grid <- expand.grid(.fL=c(0), .usekernel=c(FALSE))
# train the model
model <- train(Species~., data=iris, trControl=train_control, method="nb", tuneGrid=grid)
# summarize results
print(model)
```
I want to apply arules `discretizeDF.supervised` (https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/arulesCBA/versions/1.1.4/topics/discretizeDF.supervised)  using only the training fold to learn the correct groups and then apply it to the test fold. I don't mind using any other library/function for discretization as long as it is supervised.

AFAIK this is the correct way to do discretization so it must be a way to do it. I have been reading about "recipes" but I haven't been able to make it work.

This issue is linked with: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58684710/r-caret-discretization-within-cross-validation

title: kmeans and kmedoids step functions
description:
@topepo : I've written a couple step functions (described below) that you might consider for inclusion in the package.

`step_kmeans` : conversion of numeric variables to a reduced set by averaging within a k-means cluster partitioning of them. 
   
`step_kmedoids` : conversion of numeric variables to a reduced set by selecting the medoids from a k-medoids cluster partitioning.

Both are dimension reduction techniques that can be viewed as projections to a reduced number of components (`num_comp`), like `step_pca`.  `k_medoids` can additionally be viewed as variable selection, like `step_corr`.

The source code is available [here](https://github.com/brian-j-smith/recipes/commit/fa22b1fed16b54735a2d20449830369e551a7bfb).

Feel free to let me know if you are open to a PR for these and, if so, whether you have any questions on or suggested changes to the implementations.

title: changes in role operations
description:
Can @DavisVaughan and @EmilHvitfeldt review these changes in the `formula-mods` branch? They are related to #283 and #284? 

```r
devtools::install_github("tidymodels/recipes", ref = "formula-mods")

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

library(recipes)
data(biomass)

# Using the formula method, roles are created for any outcomes and predictors:
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  summary()

# However `sample` and `dataset` aren't predictors. Since they already have
# roles, `update_role()` can be used to make changes:
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  summary()

# `udpate_role()` can only effect one role at a time and cannot set a role to NA
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  summary()

# `udpate_role()` can only effect one role at a time and cannot set a role to NA
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  summary()

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# You can have variables be more than one role. `add_role()` can be used
# if the column already has at least one role:
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  add_role(carbon, sulfur, new_role = "something") %>%
  summary()

# `udpate_role()` has an argument called `old_role` that is used when the
# column currently has multiple roles.
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  add_role(carbon, sulfur, new_role = "something") %>%
  update_role(carbon, old_role = "something", new_role = "something else") %>%
  summary()

# `carbon` has two roles at the end, so the last `update_roles()` fails since
# `old_role` was not given.
# recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
#   update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
#   update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
#   add_role(carbon, sulfur, new_role = "something") %>%
#   update_role(carbon, new_role = "something else") %>%
#   summary()

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# To remove a role, `remove_role()` can be used to affect a single role.
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  add_role(carbon, sulfur, new_role = "something") %>%
  remove_role(carbon, old_role = "something") %>%
  summary()

# To remove all roles, call `remove_role()` multiple times to reset to `NA`
recipe(HHV ~ ., data = biomass) %>%
  update_role(sample, new_role = "id variable") %>%
  update_role(dataset, new_role = "splitting variable") %>%
  add_role(carbon, new_role = "something") %>%
  remove_role(carbon, old_role = "something") %>%
  remove_role(carbon, old_role = "predictor") %>%
  summary()

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# If the formula method is not used, all columns have a missing role:
recipe(biomass) %>%
  summary()
```

title: text recipe steps
Oblique principle components clustering / varclust step?
description:
I'm curious if a step for [oblique principle components clustering][1] would see much use:

```r
step_varclus(recipe, ...)
```

I'm not sure if many people would use this, but Harrell pushes it pretty hard in his book and [`Hmisc::varclus()`][2] implements something related (a quick look seems to me like just hierarchical clustering on top of a similarity matrix but no oblique rotation?). So far as I know that's the only R implementation, although there's also [PROC varclus][3] in SAS.

Mostly I'm just curious how well this sort of thing works. If it gets used a lot in biostats might be worth having a step for, and also potentially including in the feature engineering book.

Would love to see this written up into a small package for people to experiment with. Doesn't seem like that much work but would want to see enthusiasm/interest from others before starting to take that on.

[1]: https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ton_Schaik/publication/242249665_A_Note_on_Oblique_Principal_Component_Cluster_Analysis/links/0c960520b7323d2cc3000000/A-Note-on-Oblique-Principal-Component-Cluster-Analysis.pdf
[2]: https://github.com/harrelfe/Hmisc/blob/master/R/varclus.s
[3]: https://www.listendata.com/2015/03/proc-varclus-explained.html

title: leverage values
description:
Compute the hat values of a data point. `prep` would compute `A = inv(X'X)` (or the QR decomposition) so that the `bake` method could create a new column that is `x'Ax`. Perhaps default its role to "diagnostic" or something similar. 

`stats` has some functionality but it doesn't work for new data points and is only implemented for `lm` objects. We could fake an `lm` objects but that is probably more work than we need. 

Maybe all them hat values since there is no regression going on.

title: Dummies when the values may be in many columns
description:
Maybe I missed how to do this in the documentation, but it'd be nice to have a step for creating dummies when the values may be held in multiple columns.  For example, diagnosis codes may be in many columns (Secondary Dx 1--X) but we don't really care which one it's in. 

My usual (messy) workflow for this would be something like: 

``` r
library(reshape2)
df <- rbind.data.frame( c('a', 'b', 'c'), c('d', 'a', 'c'), c('b', 'd', 'a'), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
colnames(df) <- c('v1', 'v2', 'v3')

head(df)
#>   v1 v2 v3
#> 1  a  b  c
#> 2  d  a  c
#> 3  b  d  a

df$id <- c(1,2,3)


df2 <- dcast( melt(df ,id.var='id'), 
              id ~ value, 
              length)

head(df2)
#>   id a b c d
#> 1  1 1 1 1 0
#> 2  2 1 0 1 1
#> 3  3 1 1 0 1

title: Invertible transformations
description:
In essence recipes currently define a forward map. You `fit()` the forward map with `prep()` and apply it to data with `bake()`. The backwards direction should work the same way, i.e. you should just apply some generic like `unbake()` to the data.

But now there are these issues of fidelity in the recovery. Three possibilities:

- all steps are invertible (i.e. centering, scaling, etc) and allow perfect recovery
- the steps are pseudo-invertible (i.e PCA where you drop terms)
- the steps just aren't invertible (t-SNE)

The last two should definitely error or give a warning. This would also require modifying all the `prep()` methods to learn the backwards map at `prep()` time (i.e. when you `prep()` a PCA-step, if you support inversion, you now need to save the information associated with the back transform, which is distinct from the information associated with the forward transform).

Side-note: these generics have nice analogues in the `sklearn` world:

- `prep()` is `fit()`
- `juice()` is `fit_transform()`
- `bake()` is `transform()`
- `unbake()` would be `untransform()`, although I'm not sure how many inverse transformations (if any) are support for `sklearn`

title: Custom step work fine while baking but not while used in caret::train
description:
I developped a custom step in order to include it in some caret models.  While applying prep and bake on my new step, everything works fine. But when I try to include the unprepared recipe in caret::train I got the following error: "Error: No variables or terms were selected". Any advice welcome. 
Reproducible example and session info hereunder: 

```
packs <- c("tidyverse", "caret", "e1071", "wavelets", "recipes")
InstIfNec<-function (pack) {
    if (!do.call(require,as.list(pack))) {
        do.call(install.packages,as.list(pack)) }
    do.call(require,as.list(pack)) }
lapply(packs, InstIfNec)
```

# Getting data
```
data(biomass)
biomass<-select(biomass, -dataset, -sample)
```

# Custom pretreatment algo
```
HaarTransform<-function(DF1) {
    w<-function(k) { 
        s1=dwt(k, filter="haar")
        return (s1@V[[1]])
    }
    Smt=as.matrix(DF1)
    Smt=t(base::apply(Smt,1,w))
    return (data.frame(Smt))
}
```

# Create the custum step function
```
step_Haar_new<-function(terms=NULL, role=NA, trained=FALSE, skip=FALSE, 
                        columns=NULL) {
    step(subclass="Haar",  terms=terms, role=role,
         trained=trained, skip=skip, columns=columns)
}

step_Haar<-function(recipe, ..., role=NA, trained=FALSE, skip=FALSE,
                    columns=NULL) {
    terms=ellipse_check(...)
    add_step(recipe, 
             step_Haar_new(terms=terms, role=role, trained=trained,  
                           skip=skip, columns=columns))
}

prep.step_Haar <- function(x, training, info = NULL, ...) {
    col_names<-terms_select(terms = x$terms, info = info)
    step_Haar_new(terms = x$terms,  role = x$role, trained = TRUE, 
                  skip = x$skip, columns=col_names)
}

bake.step_Haar <- function(object, new_data, ...) {
    new_data<-HaarTransform(dplyr::select(new_data, object$columns))
    as_tibble(new_data)
}
```


# Test the recipe function
```
Haar_recipe<-recipe(carbon ~ ., biomass) %>% 
    step_Haar(all_predictors()) 

Haar_recipe%>%
    prep(biomass) %>%
    bake(biomass)   # all is fine

fit <- caret::train(Haar_recipe, data=biomass,
                    method="svmLinear")  # Error: No variables or terms were selected.`
```

title: propose to change step_ica() default option to use "method = 'C'"
description:
## Short version

`step_ICA` using `options = list(method = 'C')` is always faster than the default `method = 'R`, with no downsides.
I don't know what the policy is on changing  external package defaults in `recipes`, but it's a 'free' speed gain.

## Longer version

`step_ica` uses `fastICA::fastICA` which has an argument `method`. Quoting FastICA's documentation:

> if method == "R" then computations are done exclusively in R (default). The code allows the interested R user to see exactly what the algorithm does. if method == "C" then C code is used to perform most of the computations, which makes the algorithm run faster. During compilation the C code is linked to an optimized BLAS library if present, otherwise stand-alone BLAS routines are compiled.

So in almost all cases, you want `method = 'C'`. The only use for 'R' seem to be the very specific case where you want to see the exact calculations - but then you would have to look in the documentation for `step_ica` anyway (and see the changed default).

So I propose to change the default option of `step_ica` to use `method = 'C'`. I can make a pull request (at some point) if you want.

Below is a small example of the speed gain. Note that it varies but is consistently positive.

``` r
library('fastICA')
library('tictoc')
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(runif(5e6), 5e6 / 20, 20)
tic()
a <- fastICA(X, 20, method = "R")
toc()
#> 4.177 sec elapsed
tic()
b <- fastICA(X, 20, method = "C")
toc()
#> 2.629 sec elapsed
```

title: Better error for prepping a tunable recipe
description:
Hi, thank you very much for `recipes`! Your work is very valuable to me and the community.

I was pondering whether tunable recipes should always return a standard error when a user tries to `prep` a tunable recipe. From my experience, any all tunable recipes will return an error when `prep`ped. Perhaps it can be a standard error. For example:

`Error: tunable recipes cannot be used with `prep`. Did you want to tune the recipe?`

I'm not sure that's the most informative error since you can tune the recipe with several tuning functions but something along those lines would be informative.

title: Error while passing an empty vector of column names to step_xyz()
description:
Is there a way to pass a vector of column names to a step_xyz() function such that there's no error even if the vector is empty?

For instance, I would like to perform different kinds of imputations on different columns. Let the columns names be - col1, col2, and col3. I want to perform mean imputation on col1, median imputation on col2, and KNN imputation on col3. 

But instead of hardcoding the columns, I want them to be an input. So, I create 3 vectors - col_mean_impute, col_median_impute, and col_knn_impute. And then I add all three to the same recipe object like this - 
```
recipe_obj <- rec %>% 
    step_mean(col_mean_impute) %>%
    step_median(col_median_impute) %>%
    step_knn(col_knn_impute) %>%
```

The catch is, any of these vectors could be empty. Currently,  I get an error - `No variables or terms were selected.`. 

Is there a way around this?

title: step_nzv can create surprises downstream
description:
When using `recipes` programmatically, we might not know what columns `step_nzv` will remove. If it removes all nominal columns and there's a step for nominals downstream, it breaks. A general solution that would make the package more flexible would be to let prepping go through even if no columns are selected, and just have the step not do anything. I'd be happy to work on that if you want.

``` r
library(recipes)
d <- data.frame(x = c(rep("a", 29), 'B'), y = rnorm(30))
recipe(d, y ~ x) %>%
  step_nzv(all_nominal()) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal()) %>%
  prep(d)
#> Error: No variables or terms were selected.
```

title: preped recipe requires 1000x more space when saved as a RDS from within a function than from "plain code"
description:
The code below creates 2 .RDS files.
"temp.rds"  is created from plain code and requires 5 KB.
"temp2.rds" is created from the same code wrapped inside a function and requires 5  284 KB

does anyone have any idea?  This code is inspired from this issue https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/301

```
library(rlang)
  library(recipes)
  library(dplyr)

big_iris <- bind_rows(rep_along(1:1000, list(as_tibble(iris))))

rec_small <- recipe(Sepal.Length ~ Species + Sepal.Width, big_iris[0,]) %>%
  step_center(Sepal.Width)

p_rec_small <- prep(rec_small, big_iris, retain = FALSE)
readr::write_rds(p_rec_small, "temp.rds") # 5kb

myfunction <- function(){
  big_iris <- bind_rows(rep_along(1:1000, list(as_tibble(iris))))

  rec_small <- recipe(Sepal.Length ~ Species + Sepal.Width, big_iris[0,]) %>%
    step_center(Sepal.Width)
  
  p_rec_small <- prep(rec_small, big_iris, retain = FALSE)

  readr::write_rds(p_rec_small, "temp2.rds") # 5284kb  BIG
  
}

myfunction()
```

title: trouble with `update_role` then `step_dummy` on character/factor col
description:
I'm having trouble with `update_role` when the ID column is a character column. In the example below, I get coefficient estimates for `ID`, even after its role is updated, and moreover, no estimates for levels of `GRADE`. Same issue if I mutate the `ID` col to a factor. However, if I mutate the `ID` col to `1:10` then the model works as it should (`FLAGGED ~ MARK + GRADE`), but in my real-world use case, I'd prefer to keep the IDs as they are. 

I think the issue is related to then using `all_nominal()` as an input to `step_dummy` since `ID` is nominal. If I just use `step_dummy(GRADE)` the problem goes away. And whilst that's fine for this toy example, it would be a pain to name all the variables in my real world dataset. And whilst you can use the selector `-all_outcomes()` to remove outcomes from `step_dummy`, I can't see an equivalent selector to remove all IDs.

Not sure if this is a bug, a feature, or me doing something wrong.

I'm running macOS 10.15.5, R 4.0.2 and RStudio 1.3.959.

title: recipes is very strict about required columns
description:
Imagine I have a big dataset, I pre-process with recipes, I estimate a model and then remove unused variables. Then, for new data, I want to apply the pre-processing recipe (`bake()`), but it won't work if not all columns are in the dataset (which is the point of pruning). This is shown in the below example taken from the `step_integer()` documentation: 

``` r

  step_integer(all_predictors()) %>%

title: Replace missing values with a constant
description:
There is a need for NA values imputation with a constant. For some models constant number imputation usually would work better than median or other type of imputations. For example, in neural network models, NA value replacement with zeros works well as the nodes with input values equal to 0 do not send any further signals. And, in the tree-based models, some extreme value imputations (such as "-99999") is suitable as the tree models will make separate splits for these extreme values. 

Please, can a constant number imputation step be implemented in the R recipes?

Thanks.

title: Use glmnet with tidymodels.

Code below:

library(tidymodels)

preprocess <- recipe(price~., data = diamonds_df)

glmnet_model <- linear_reg(
  mode    = "regression",
  penalty = tune(),
  mixture = tune()

  set_engine("glmnet")

glmnet_wfl <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(preprocess) %>%
  add_model(glmnet_model)

glmnet_params <- parameters(penalty(), mixture())

glmnet_grid <- grid_max_entropy(glmnet_params, size = 20)

glmnet_cv_result <- tune_grid(
  glmnet_wfl,
  resamples = diamonds_cv2,
  grid = glmnet_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(mae, mape, rmse, rsq),

title: Interacting with a categorical variable
description:
In a standard model.matrix call I can interact a variable `V1` with a categorical variable `label` using `Class ~ V1 * label`

Under the hoods, label is expanded into multiple columns using one hot encoding, and those columns will be called `labelB`, `labelC` etc. Throughout the process I do not need to worry about the function changing the name. 

Using recipes, what is the right set up for using step_dummy and step_interact together? If I call for the interaction V1:label in step_interact, I have to process `label` using step_dummy first. By doing so, I have to keep track of the fact that after step_dummy, there is no longer a column named `label`, and therefore I cannot use that name in step_interact.

```r
data("Sonar")
Sonar = cbind(Sonar, label = c(rep("A", 104), rep("B", 104)))

sonar_rec <- recipe(Class ~ ., data = Sonar) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal())# %>%
  #step_interact(~ V1:label)
  
prep(sonar_rec, Sonar) %>% bake(Sonar)
```

title: Aggregating rows after a step_dummy : a custom step_summarize and wider issues
description:
I'm opening an issue following a suggestion from @juliasilge on StackOverflow (the [question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/63372731/4653440), her [suggestion](https://stackoverflow.com/a/63474617/4653440)).

It is both a feature request and a possible bug report. It probably belongs to several repo at once.

The crux of the issue is in the three datasets below. A dataset needs to be modified from long to wide during a recipe, preventing the use of a pivot before the preprocessing.
```
#initial df
    #> # A tibble: 5 x 2
    #>   name  color 
    #>   <chr> <chr> 
    #> 1 A     green 
    #> 2 A     yellow
    #> 3 A     purple
    #> 4 B     green 
    #> 5 C     blue

# dummified df
    #> # A tibble: 5 x 5
    #>   name  color_blue color_green color_purple color_yellow
    #>   <fct>      <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
    #> 1 A              0           1            0            0
    #> 2 A              0           0            0            1
    #> 3 A              0           0            1            0
    #> 4 B              0           1            0            0
    #> 5 C              1           0            0            0

# deduplicated df
    #> # A tibble: 3 x 5
    #>   name  color_blue color_green color_purple color_yellow
    #>   <fct>      <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
    #> 1 A              0           1            1            1
    #> 2 B              0           1            0            0
    #> 3 C              1           0            0            0
```

I hope the commented reprex below is clear and detailed enough to explain everything. 

``` r
# Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
#> ── Attaching packages ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels 0.1.0 ──
#> ✓ broom     0.5.6      ✓ rsample   0.0.7 
#> ✓ dials     0.0.7      ✓ tune      0.1.0 
#> ✓ infer     0.5.2      ✓ workflows 0.1.1 
#> ✓ parsnip   0.1.2      ✓ yardstick 0.0.6 
#> ✓ recipes   0.1.13
#> ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels_conflicts() ──
#> x scales::discard() masks purrr::discard()
#> x dplyr::filter()   masks stats::filter()
#> x recipes::fixed()  masks stringr::fixed()
#> x dplyr::lag()      masks stats::lag()
#> x yardstick::spec() masks readr::spec()
#> x recipes::step()   masks stats::step()
library(modeldata)

data(ames)


# I'll reconstruct a dataset showcasing the real life behaviour I'm encoutering.

# I'll use Lot_Area as my ID, because there are duplicated rows
ames %>% nrow()
#> [1] 2930
ames %>% distinct(Lot_Area) %>% nrow()
#> [1] 1960

# Each ID only has a single possible numeric value
int_variables <- ames %>% 
    select(Lot_Area, Sale_Price, Total_Bsmt_SF) %>% 
    group_by(Lot_Area) %>% 
    summarise(across(everything(), mean))
#> `summarise()` ungrouping output (override with `.groups` argument)

# But each ID can have duplicated rows because the dataset is in a long format and each ID can have several Neighborhood or MS_Zoning (in a real life use case, those variables would be embedding for instance), resulting in several rows.

reconstructed_dataset <- ames %>% 
    select(Lot_Area, Neighborhood, MS_Zoning) %>% 
    inner_join(int_variables) %>%
    distinct()
#> Joining, by = "Lot_Area"

# We have 223 ID with duplicated rows
ames %>% 
    mutate(aggregated_factors = paste(Neighborhood, MS_Zoning)) %>% 
    select(Lot_Area, aggregated_factors) %>% 
    group_by(Lot_Area) %>% 
    summarise(across(everything(), n_distinct)) %>% 
    filter(aggregated_factors > 1)
#> `summarise()` ungrouping output (override with `.groups` argument)
#> # A tibble: 223 x 2
#>    Lot_Area aggregated_factors
#>       <int>              <int>
#>  1     1890                  2
#>  2     2160                  2
#>  3     2280                  2
#>  4     3000                  2
#>  5     3182                  2
#>  6     3500                  2
#>  7     3880                  2
#>  8     3940                  2
#>  9     4060                  2
#> 10     4280                  2
#> # … with 213 more rows


# Now we'll have to create the initial split
# We need a custom function, because we want the same IDs to be in the same groups
# The custom function is not ideal, because the size of the groups is balanced while counting the duplicated rows

inital_split_id <- function(data, group, prop = 3/4) {
    group_vfold_cv(data,
                   {{group}},
                   1/(1-prop)) %>%
        head(1) %>%
        pull(1) %>%
        pluck(1)
}

set.seed(42)

te_tr_split_gp <- reconstructed_dataset %>% inital_split_id(group = Lot_Area)

reconstructed_df_train_int <- training(te_tr_split_gp)
reconstructed_df_test_int <- testing(te_tr_split_gp)

# Now we can create our recipe
ames_recipe <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = reconstructed_df_train_int) %>% 
    update_role(Lot_Area, new_role = "id variable") %>% 
    step_normalize(Sale_Price, Total_Bsmt_SF) %>% 
    step_other(Neighborhood, MS_Zoning, threshold = 0.05) %>%
    step_dummy(Neighborhood, MS_Zoning)

# step_dummy preceded by step_other prevent us from using a simpler solution, which would be to pivot the wole dataset before applying the recipe to it.

prepped_ames_recipe <- ames_recipe %>%
    prep(training = reconstructed_df_train_int)

reconstructed_df_train <- prepped_ames_recipe %>% 
    juice()

# the prepped df still has the duplicated rows, so we'll create a custom step below to summarize them

step_summarize <- function(recipe,
                           ...,
                           role = NA,
                           trained = FALSE,
                           col_names = NULL,
                           skip = FALSE,
                           id = rand_id("summarize")) {
    terms <- ellipse_check(...)
    
    add_step(
        recipe,
        step_summarize_new(
            terms = terms,
            role = role,
            trained = trained,
            col_names = col_names,
            skip = skip,
            id = id
        )
    )
}


step_summarize_new <-
    function(terms, role, trained, col_names, skip, id) {
        step(
            subclass = "summarize",
            terms = terms,
            role = role,
            trained = trained,
            col_names = col_names,
            skip = skip,
            id = id
        )
    }

prep.step_summarize <- function(x, training, info = NULL, ...) {
    col_names <- terms_select(terms = x$terms, info = info)
    
    step_summarize_new(
        terms = x$terms,
        trained = TRUE,
        role = x$role,
        col_names = col_names,
        skip = x$skip,
        id = x$id
    )
}


bake.step_summarize <- function(object, new_data, ...) {
    vars <- object$col_names
    
    new_data <- new_data %>%
        group_by(across(-any_of(vars))) %>%
        summarise(across(any_of(vars), ~ ifelse(max(.) > 0, 1, 0)))
    
    tibble::as_tibble(new_data)
}

# the new recipe step
ames_recipe_f <- recipe(Sale_Price ~ ., data = reconstructed_df_train_int) %>% 
    update_role(Lot_Area, new_role = "id variable") %>% 
    step_normalize(Sale_Price, Total_Bsmt_SF) %>% 
    step_other(Neighborhood, MS_Zoning, threshold = 0.05) %>%
    step_dummy(Neighborhood, MS_Zoning) %>% 
    step_summarize(c(starts_with("Neighborhood"), starts_with("MS_Zoning")))

prepped_ames_recipe_f <- ames_recipe_f %>%
    prep(training = reconstructed_df_train_int)
#> `summarise()` regrouping output by 'Lot_Area', 'Total_Bsmt_SF' (override with `.groups` argument)

#extracting the reduced training set
reconstructed_df_train <- prepped_ames_recipe_f %>% 
    juice()

#extracting the reduced testing set
reconstructed_df_test <- reconstructed_df_test_int %>% 
    bake(prepped_ames_recipe_f, new_data = .)
#> `summarise()` regrouping output by 'Lot_Area', 'Sale_Price' (override with `.groups` argument)

# Both of the sets correctly have their rows deduplicated
reconstructed_df_train_int %>% filter(Lot_Area == 6000)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   Lot_Area Neighborhood               MS_Zoning         Sale_Price Total_Bsmt_SF
#>      <int> <fct>                      <fct>                  <dbl>         <dbl>

#> 4     6000 South_and_West_of_Iowa_St… Residential_Low_…    122029.          787.
reconstructed_df_train %>% filter(Lot_Area == 6000)

#> #   Neighborhood_Gilbert <dbl>, Neighborhood_Sawyer <dbl>,
#> #   Neighborhood_other <dbl>, MS_Zoning_Residential_Medium_Density <dbl>,
#> #   MS_Zoning_other <dbl>
    
reconstructed_df_test_int %>% filter(Lot_Area == 5000)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 5
#>   Lot_Area Neighborhood               MS_Zoning         Sale_Price Total_Bsmt_SF
#>      <int> <fct>                      <fct>                  <dbl>         <dbl>

#> 2     5000 South_and_West_of_Iowa_St… Residential_Low_…     97756.          709.
#> 3     5000 Brookside                  Residential_Low_…     97756.          709.
#> 4     5000 Iowa_DOT_and_Rail_Road     Residential_Medi…     97756.          709.
#> 5     5000 Old_Town                   Residential_Medi…     97756.          709.
reconstructed_df_test %>% filter(Lot_Area == 5000)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 13
#>   Lot_Area Total_Bsmt_SF Sale_Price Neighborhood_Co… Neighborhood_Ol…
#>      <int>         <dbl>      <dbl>            <dbl>            <dbl>

#> #   Neighborhood_Somerset <dbl>, Neighborhood_Northridge_Heights <dbl>,

#> #   Neighborhood_other <dbl>, MS_Zoning_Residential_Medium_Density <dbl>,
#> #   MS_Zoning_other <dbl>

# Sadly, we'll encounter other problems down the line.

# First, let's define a simple model that we will want to tune

engine_rf <- rand_forest(
    mode = "regression",
    mtry = tune(),
    trees = tune(),
    min_n = 5
) %>% 
    set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity")

# We can then create a workflow

reg_workflow <- workflow() %>% 
    add_recipe(ames_recipe_f) %>% 
    add_model(engine_rf)

# To create the resampling groups for the tuning, we'll need another custom function

custom_group_vfold_cv <- function(data, v = 5, repeats = 3, group = NULL){
    
    if (!missing(group)) {
        group <- tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!enquo(group))
        if (length(group) == 0) {
            group <- NULL
        }
    }
    if (is.null(group) || !is.character(group) || length(group) != 
        1) 
        stop("`group` should be a single character value for the column ", 
             "that will be used for splitting.", call. = FALSE)
    if (!any(names(data) == group)) 
        stop("`group` should be a column in `data`.", call. = FALSE)
    
    
    if (repeats == 1) {
        split_objs <- rsample:::group_vfold_splits(data = data, group = group, 
                                                   v = v)
    }
    else {
        for (i in 1:repeats) {
            tmp <- rsample:::group_vfold_splits(data = data, group = group, 
                                                v = v)
            tmp$id2 <- tmp$id
            tmp$id <- names0(repeats, "Repeat")[i]
            split_objs <- if (i == 1) 
                tmp
            else rbind(split_objs, tmp)
        }
    }
    split_objs$splits <- map(split_objs$splits, rsample:::rm_out)
    cv_att <- list(v = v, repeats = repeats, group = group)
    new_rset(splits = split_objs$splits, ids = split_objs[, grepl("^id", 
                                                                  names(split_objs))], attrib = cv_att, subclass = c("rset"))
    
}

# We need to work on the training set before its preprocessing by the recipe.
# By doing so with this simple function that doesn't take this into account, 
# we may end up with wildly imbalanced groups.

tuning_grid <- grid_random(
    mtry() %>% range_set(c(1, 5)),
    trees() %>% range_set(c(10, 11)), 
    size = 5
)

# Let's tune the workflow
tuning_res <- tune_grid(
    reg_workflow,
    resamples = train_cv,
    grid = tuning_grid,
    control = control_grid(save_pred = TRUE)
)

train_cv_alt <- custom_group_vfold_cv(reconstructed_df_train, group = Lot_Area, v = 2, repeats = 2)

tuning_res <- tune_grid(
    engine_rf,

My custom step is probably wrong somewhere, but if it isn't, then custom steps may not be correctly taken into account by the whole tidymodels ecosystem. 
I often encounter this kind of dataset structure in real life, making it hard to use any kind of pipeline workflow. I don't know if I'm the only one.
I see several problems : if custom steps sometimes don't work later on during tuning for instance, it is obviously problematic. But even having this kind of step directly in the package, either as a specific step or as an option in step_dummy for instance, we will still have the resampling issues during the initial split or the folds creation.
And at the same time, `recipes` and the whole `tidymodels` ecosystem obviously are supposed to be applied on tidy data. Which make it hard when the tidyfication and the preprocessing of the dataset can't be done in two distincts steps.

title: Feature: as.data.frame
description:
recipes have a great potential within the R ecosystem. But as discussed in [this question](https://github.com/tidymodels/recipes/issues/543) it seems that `juice` and `prep` are not well received by some users. 

In a subset of very used functions `as.data.frame` is used in cases where `data` arguments are assumed to be `data.frame`'s. One method for letting recipes be more versatile and useful across myriad of packages (without **any** alterations from the package author!) is to simply have a `as.data.frame` method for recipes, which could call `juice(self)` to return the training dataset. 

One such scenario would be for back-compatibility with the existing `model.matrix` and similar functions, which would allow users to do some preprocessing with `recipe` but give a different way to use these outside `tidymodels` for functions that may not be implemented in this ecosystem yet.

A very simple example:
```R
library(recipes)
as.data.frame.recipe <- function(x, ...)
   juice(x)
data(iris)
rec <- recipe(iris)  %>% step_center(all_numeric()) %>% prep()
model.matrix(Species ~ ., data = rec)
```

Another useful example:
```R
library(recipes)
as.data.frame.recipe <- function(x, ...)
   juice(x)
data(mtcars)
rec <- recipe(mtcars) %>% step_center(all_numeric()) %>% prep()
library(e1071)
svm(mpg ~ cyl + hp, data = rec)
```

While this doesn't incentivize the use of tidymodels, it makes the usability much greater for the package.

title: Profiling time spend at each step
description:
This is not much of an issue and more for future users having the same problem as me.

Problem: Finding out how much time is spend in each step of the recipe. Figuring out which steps are slow.

Solution: I wrote this little function

``` r

library(tidyverse)

recipe_prof <- function(expr, rate = 0.01) {
  prof_output <- tempfile()
  Rprof(prof_output, interval = rate)
  expr
  Rprof(NULL)
  
  second_scale <- function(rate) {
    function(x) {
      paste0(x * rate, "s")
    }
  }
  
  lines <- read_lines(prof_output)
  
  layer1 <- lines %>%
    str_extract("bake.step|prep.step") %>%
    replace_na("other") %>%
    str_extract("^[[:alnum:]]+")
  
  split(lines, layer1) %>%
    map_dfr(~ list(step = str_extract(.x, "step_[[:alnum:]]+")), .id = "layer") %>%
    ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = step)) +
    geom_bar() +
    facet_wrap(~ layer) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = second_scale(rate)) +
    labs(y = "time")
}
```

that you can then wrap around your prep line to get the time spend baking and prepping.

```r
library(tidymodels)

big_diamods <- sample_n(diamonds, 400000, replace = TRUE)

rec <- recipe(price ~ ., data = big_diamods) %>%
  step_dummy(cut, color, clarity) %>%
  step_scale(all_numeric()) %>%
  step_center(all_numeric()) %>%
  step_pca(all_numeric())


recipe_prof(
  prepped <- prep(rec)
)
```

title: Add `step_cut` or equivalent
description:
`discretize` as it's currently implemented, isn't quite equivalent to base R's `cut` function, in that in the latter you can specify explicit cutpoints _or_ a single integer reflecting the number of intervals.  For interpretability of variables, it's often useful to set boundaries that are more "human readable". Would it be worth it to add a `step_cut` discretization alternative and/or build that capability into the core function itself, a la `cut`.

Since recipes are often meant to be used with multiple variables, this may not ideal, so an alternative is some sort of rounding parameters for cleaner breaks (ie round to neareast N).

title: New function name for juice()
description:
We have a set of "verbs" to use with recipes:

![recipes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/master/rstats-artwork/recipes.png)

- First you specify a dataset and variables.
- Next you add preprocessing **steps**.
- Then you **prep** the recipe to estimate the quantities for each step from the training data.
- Finally, you can apply this prepped recipe to new data with **bake**.

[Feedback from users](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62189885/what-is-the-difference-among-prep-bake-juice-in-the-r-package-recipes/62205555#62205555) indicates that there is confusion around `prep()`, `bake()`, but _especially_ [`juice()`](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/reference/juice.html). The `juice()` function goes back to the prepped recipe and gets out the original training set with all steps applied. It is useful because the prepped recipe does have this information in it already. 

In almost all cases these two are the same, where `rec_prep` is a prepped recipe:

```r
juice(rec_rep)
bake(rec_prep, new_data = training_data)
```

Let's consider creating a new function that does the same thing `juice()` does, but with a new name. The `juice()` function will stay around but probably eventually be labeled "superseded".

title: Integrate arbitrary pre-processing function into a recipe
description:
One great advantage of the `{workflows}` package is - obviously - that model and pre-processing can be bundled. For arbitrary pre-processing of columns, I can use `recipes::step_mutate()`, `recipes::step_filter()` etc., although this approach is a bit limiting (I can't use arbitrary R code). However, if I have one pre-processing function `f()` that takes my datatframe (and not just a column vector of it) and that does not estimate anything and really just performs data cleaning, it would be handy if I could integrate such a function into a recipe. Otherwise, I have to carry that function along (similar to what I'd to do with a recipe if I would not use `{workflows}`). In particular, if such a function manipulates `data` with pure dplyr code, we can leverage dbplyr to execute the code also on a database, which is not possible if we use `{recipes}` functions like `recipes::step_mutate()`. So from a point of portability and flexibility, it would be desirable to do something like:
```r
basic_cleaning <- function(data) {
  # arbitrary data transformation
}
library(recipes)
rec(...) %>%
  step_lambda(basic_cleaning)
```

I am aware that this has the potential to be misused, namely if the function contains transformations that modify the input data depending on the input data. This had to be made very clear in the documentation in case you want to support this feature. However, the problem already exists with `step_mutate()`, e.g. when I use `step_mutate(z = (x - mean(x))/sd(x))` to standardise my variable instead of using `recipes::step_normalize()` I leak information from the test data set when used for inference. For this reason, in any case, I think the docs of `step_mutate()` should contain a warning.

title: Suggestion to use tidyselect as recipes selection API
description:
Hi,

I love the `{recipes}` package but I still find myself confused about the best way to select variables for a given step. I often forget whether the variables selected for a step are the intersection or the union of the selectors passed to `...`. I also find it to be a slightly extra amount of mental friction that often I find myself selecting variables I want by defining the variables I __don't__ want.

For example, if I want to apply a step to all numeric predictors, the way I usually do it is by selecting numeric NOT outcomes. It just feels a little backwards to me.
```r
recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes())
```
I'm wondering if it should be possible to nest the selector functions to form AND statements, and then comma separated selectors passed to `...` be the OR statements. The suggested API would look something like:
```r
recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors(all_numeric()))

# or via the pipe
recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric() %>% all_predictors())
```
This may just be a _me_ problem, but I think it could be a nice addition and allow for more intuitive specifications of variable selections within steps. It wouldn't be a breaking change, I don't think, the selectors would just need to accept `...` as an arbitrary number of additional selectors. 

Perhaps to really ramp up the selection possibilities, the role selectors could even accept tidy selectors:
```r
recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors(ends_with("p"))) # select disp and hp among predictors
```

title: step_pls fails to work when the outcome is not numeric
description:
I don't think that always makes sense - best would be if step_pls could convert factor levels internally to integers without throwing an error.

Small example:

```
iris_filter <- iris %>% 
  filter(Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor")) %>% 
  mutate(Species = factor(Species, levels = c("setosa", "versicolor")))

rec <- iris_filter %>% 
  recipe(Species ~ ., ) %>% 
  step_pls(all_numeric(), outcome = "Species")
```

```
prep(rec, retain = TRUE)
Error: All columns selected for the step should be numeric
```

Otherwise we would need to do something like this to prevent that:
```
rec <- iris_filter %>% 
  recipe(Species ~ ., ) %>% 
  step_mutate(Species = ifelse(Species == "setosa", 1, 0)) %>% 
  step_pls(all_numeric(), outcome = "Species") %>% 
  step_mutate(Species = ifelse(Species == 1, "setosa", "versicolor"))
```

```

Data Recipe

   outcome          1
 predictor          4

Training data contained 100 data points and no missing data.

Operations:

Variable mutation for  Species [trained]

title: FR: step_neglog()
description:
This is a feature request for a Neglog transformation step. The formula is `sign(x) * log(abs(x) + 1)`. 

This would be similar to using `step_log(signed = TRUE, offset = 1)`, but without the restriction that `signed = TRUE` means that the offset is ignored. 

This is a transformation I use with variables that include negative values and where those values in (-1, 1) need to be preserved in some form (whereas `step_log(signed = TRUE)` sets them to 0). 

I have written the code to do this, so I'd be happy to create a pull request. As per the [contributor guide](https://www.tidymodels.org/contribute/) I first wanted to check whether this feature seems reasonable to you. Of course even if you think it's a good idea I guess you might prefer allowing `signed` and `offset` together in `step_log()`, but that might be messier and/or be too disruptive to people using that function. 

More info about the transformation and its application in Whittaker, Whitehead, and Somers 2005, [The neglog transformation and quantile regression for the analysis of a large credit scoring database](https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9876.2005.00520.x)

title: Add numbering of steps in output of `prep` to make tidy() function easier to write
description:
## Feature

In situations when using tidy subsequent to a prep step to look at model outputs, given that tidy takes an argument of which step to extract it would be helpful to number the steps in the output of prep.

Looking at the example [here](https://juliasilge.com/blog/best-hip-hop/).

### Current output
```
ranking_prep <- prep(ranking_rec)
ranking_prep

## Data Recipe
## 
## Inputs:
## 
##       role #variables
##         id          2
##    outcome          1
##  predictor         12
## 
## Training data contained 293 data points and no missing data.
## 
## Operations:
## 
## Log transformation on points [trained]
## Centering and scaling for year, danceability, energy, key, loudness, ... [trained]
## PCA extraction with year, danceability, energy, key, loudness, ... [trained]

tidied_pca <- tidy(ranking_prep, 3)
```

### Suggested output
```
ranking_prep <- prep(ranking_rec)
ranking_prep

## Data Recipe
## 
## Inputs:
## 
##       role #variables
##         id          2
##    outcome          1
##  predictor         12
## 
## Training data contained 293 data points and no missing data.
## 
## Operations:
## 
## (Step 1) Log transformation on points [trained]
## (Step 2) Centering and scaling for year, danceability, energy, key, loudness, ... [trained]
## (Step 3) PCA extraction with year, danceability, energy, key, loudness, ... [trained]

tidied_pca <- tidy(ranking_prep, 3)
```
That way it is clear where that 3 is coming from, and for complex recipes one doesn't have to manually count steps.

title: Easy Way to Map the var_info & term_info tibbles
description:

title: C-stack achieved at quickly as the number of variables increase
description:
I started looking into the recipes package, which seems to provide some incredible tools for not only preprocessing but also evaluating at a production level, if speed is not of the essence.  Especially the latter part is something that is extremely useful. 

In my current line of work however I often work around 300 variables, and this quickly turns out to be a problem for the recipes, as it hits the stack limit rather quickly

```r
library(recipes)
nmax <- 300
data <- matrix(rnorm(nmax), ncol = nmax)
data <- as.data.frame(data)
#Success vector
v <- logical(nmax - 1)
for(i in seq_len(nmax)[-1]){
  e <- try(recipe(data, reformulate(paste0('V', seq(2, i), collapse = '+'), response = 'V1')), silent = TRUE)
  v[i - 1] <- !inherits(e, 'try-error')
  rm(e)
  gc()
}
#At which point does recipes fail?
which.min(unlist(v))
# [1] 144
```

The problem seems to be how ´recipes:::fun_calls` recursively evaluates formulas.
```r
form <- reformulate(paste0('V', 2:200, collapse = '+'), 'V1')
recipes:::fun_calls(form)
#Error: C stack usage  7976588 is too close to the limit
```

while I am not entirely sure how this could be avoided, it seems like it should be possible to `split` the formula and evaluate in a less recursive way.

This was experienced in a Docker container (using `rocker/tidyverse:4.0.0`), with an allocated memory of 6 GB, 1.5 GB swap memory, 60 GB disk space and 4 CPU's.

title: `predict()` with column name that is also a function name tries to use function
description:
Using a dataframe with a column whose name is also a function name confuses the `predict()` function.  Below is an example.  It thinks the column name `ts` is the function named `ts()`.

Related is an issue where I am not getting `step_lag()` to work, even with a column name that is not a function.  See: https://stackoverflow.com/q/64338885/1022967

Possible related tickets:
https://github.com/tidymodels/tune/issues/181
https://github.com/tidymodels/tune/issues/206


``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> -- Attaching packages -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- tidymodels 0.1.1 --
#> v broom     0.7.1      v recipes   0.1.13
#> v dials     0.0.9      v rsample   0.0.8 
#> v dplyr     1.0.2      v tibble    3.0.3 
#> v ggplot2   3.3.2      v tidyr     1.1.2

#> v parsnip   0.1.3      v yardstick 0.0.7 
#> v purrr     0.3.4
#> -- Conflicts ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- tidymodels_conflicts() --
#> x purrr::discard() masks scales::discard()
#> x dplyr::filter()  masks stats::filter()
#> x dplyr::lag()     masks stats::lag()
#> x recipes::step()  masks stats::step()
library(dplyr)

set.seed(123)

### Create autocorrelated timeseries: https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/29242/17203
work_df <-
    tibble(
        ts = stats::filter(rnorm(1000), filter=rep(1,5), circular=TRUE) %>%
            as.numeric()
    )
# plot(work_df$ts)
work_df
#> # A tibble: 1,000 x 1
#>          ts
#>       <dbl>
#>  1 -0.00375
#>  2  0.589  
#>  3  0.968

#>  7  0.353

## Recipe
the_rec <-
    recipe(ts ~ ., data = work_df) %>%
    step_lag(ts, lag=1:5) %>%
    step_naomit(all_predictors())

the_rec %>% prep() %>% juice()
#> # A tibble: 995 x 6

## Model
rf_mod <-

title: step_novel won't work after step_unknown: bug or feature
description:
Hi,

(Love this package and all the work you guys are doing)

Using the reproducible example from the docs, it works:

```
library(modeldata)
data(okc)

okc_tr <- okc[1:30000,]
okc_te <- okc[30001:30006,]
okc_te$diet[3] <- "cannibalism"
okc_te$diet[4] <- "vampirism"

rec <- recipe(~ diet + location, data = okc_tr)

rec <- rec %>%
  step_novel(diet, location)
rec <- prep(rec, training = okc_tr)

processed <- bake(rec, okc_te)
tibble(old = okc_te$diet, new = processed$diet)
```
```
# A tibble: 6 x 2
  old               new              
  <chr>             <fct>            
1 vegetarian        vegetarian       
2 strictly anything strictly anything
3 cannibalism       new              
4 vampirism         new              
5 NA                NA               
6 NA                NA
```

Doing `step_novel()` then `step_unknown()` also works as expected:

```
rec <- recipe(~ diet + location, data = okc_tr)

rec <- rec %>%
    step_novel(diet, location) %>% step_unknown(diet, location)
rec <- prep(rec, training = okc_tr)

processed <- bake(rec, okc_te)
tibble(old = okc_te$diet, new = processed$diet)
```
```
# A tibble: 6 x 2
  old               new              
  <chr>             <fct>            
1 vegetarian        vegetarian       
2 strictly anything strictly anything
3 cannibalism       new              
4 vampirism         new              
5 NA                unknown          
6 NA                unknown
```

But `step_novel()` after `step_unknown()`...

```
rec <- recipe(~ diet + location, data = okc_tr)

rec <- rec %>%
    step_unknown(diet, location) %>% step_novel(diet, location)
rec <- prep(rec, training = okc_tr)

processed <- bake(rec, okc_te)
tibble(old = okc_te$diet, new = processed$diet)
```
```
# A tibble: 6 x 2
  old               new              
  <chr>             <fct>            
1 vegetarian        vegetarian       
2 strictly anything strictly anything
3 cannibalism       NA               
4 vampirism         NA               
5 NA                unknown          
6 NA                unknown
```

title: `step_pca` doesn't allow to tune `threshold`
description:
Hi!

I've been using recipes to tune `step_pca` for `num_comp` and it works well. However, whenever I try to tune using `threshold`, it doesn't work. I thought it would, because there is indeed a `threshold` object in `dials` but if I run `tunable` on a recipe with ` threshold`, it doesn't flag `threshold` as tunable.

```r
library(recipes)
#> Loading required package: dplyr
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'recipes'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     step
library(tune)
library(parsnip)
library(rsample)

rcp <-
  recipe(mtcars, mpg ~ .) %>%
  step_pca(cyl, disp, hp, num_comp = tune())

tunable(rcp)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   name     call_info        source component component_id
#>   <chr>    <list>           <chr>  <chr>     <chr>       
#> 1 num_comp <named list [3]> recipe step_pca  pca_M1I52

rcp <-
  recipe(mtcars, mpg ~ .) %>%
  step_pca(cyl, disp, hp, threshold = tune())

tunable(rcp)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   name     call_info        source component component_id
#>   <chr>    <list>           <chr>  <chr>     <chr>       
#> 1 num_comp <named list [3]> recipe step_pca  pca_W84oz
```

As expected, this doesn't allow to perform a grid search using `threshold`:

```r
lm_mod <-
  linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

mt_fold <- vfold_cv(mtcars)

title: Feature Request: step_meanimpute() enhanchment
description:
Hi,
It is possible to extend the step_meanimpute() and step_medianimpute(), to be able and compute a group-specific statistic, by providing a factor variable as an argument.

Suppose I have a dataset which lists income per profession:
it would be much more appropriate to impute rows without income based on the mean or median per profession rather than impute the value solely based on on the variable we would like to impute.

title: step_dummy is deleting the NA level
description:
It's possible (with the `exclude` argument of `factor()`) to include `NA` as a recognised level in a factor. `step_dummy()` does not recognise this.

I know I can `step_unknown()` my way around this problem, but is this the intended behaviour? I think if it is, there is the need for a special error message for this special case. The current message that `x` only has 1 factor level is confusing.

``` r
factor(c(1, NA))  # does not include NA as a level
#> [1] 1    <NA>
#> Levels: 1
factor(c(1, NA), exclude = NULL)  # includes NA as a level
#> [1] 1    <NA>
#> Levels: 1 <NA>

suppressMessages(library(recipes))

df <- data.frame(x = factor(rep(c("a", NA), 50), exclude = NULL), y = runif(100))
head(df$x)
#> [1] a    <NA> a    <NA> a    <NA>
#> Levels: a <NA>

training_df <- df[1:90, ]
testing_df <- df[91:100, ]

rec <- recipe(y~x, training_df) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_predictors())

prepped <- prep(rec)
